Claude Code 2.1.94 Deep Dive: All 28 Changes Explained

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Scope: Claude Code Changelog 2.1.94 — all 28 changes Compared with: OpenAI Codex CLI, Google Gemini CLI

1. Added Amazon Bedrock Mantle Inference Support

Section titled “1. Added Amazon Bedrock Mantle Inference Support”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Amazon Mantle is AWS’s next-generation inference infrastructure layer, designed to replace traditional Bedrock inference endpoints with lower latency and higher throughput. Previously, Claude Code only supported standard Bedrock endpoints.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Enterprise users running Claude Code on AWS who want better inference performance via Mantle
  • Set the environment variable: export CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE=1, then use Claude Code normally
  • Ideal for large-scale code generation tasks (like refactoring entire projects), as Mantle is optimized for long-context inference

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Requires AWS account with Mantle access enabled
  • May have compatibility requirements with existing Bedrock region configurations
  • The environment variable approach indicates this is still experimental

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.92: Added interactive Bedrock setup wizard
  • 2.1.86: Improved prompt cache hit rates for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry users
  • 2.1.84: Added capability detection override environment variables

Product Comparison

Section titled “Product Comparison”
  • Claude Code: Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, and now Mantle
  • Codex CLI: OpenAI API only, no direct cloud platform integration
  • Gemini CLI: Google AI API + Vertex AI, Gemini Code Assist Enterprise

Future Outlook

Section titled “Future Outlook”
  • Mantle may become the default inference path for Bedrock users once stable
  • Expect future versions to integrate Mantle into the interactive setup wizard

2. Default Effort Level Changed to High for Paid Users

Section titled “2. Default Effort Level Changed to High for Paid Users”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code introduced an effort concept (low/medium/high) controlling how deeply the model thinks. Previously all users defaulted to medium, but paid/enterprise users have higher quality expectations.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Before: Team users refactoring complex code might get shallow analysis
  • Now: Default high effort produces more thorough, complete solutions
  • Still adjustable via /effort command for quick questions

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Only affects paid users: Free/individual subscription users unchanged
  • High effort means more token consumption and faster rate limit hits
  • /effort can switch anytime — not permanently locked

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.80: Added effort frontmatter support
  • 2.1.78: Added agent frontmatter effort support
  • 2.1.76: Added /effort slash command

Product Comparison

Section titled “Product Comparison”
  • Claude Code: /effort with three levels, default changed this release
  • Codex CLI: No explicit effort control; relies on model selection
  • Gemini CLI: No direct equivalent; indirectly achieved via model routing (Flash vs Pro)

3. Compact Clickable Channel Header for Slack MCP Messages

Section titled “3. Compact Clickable Channel Header for Slack MCP Messages”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code integrates Slack via MCP. When sending messages to Slack channels, the UI now shows a clean, clickable channel header instead of raw JSON.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Ask Claude Code to send a deployment notice to #dev-updates
  • Tool call area now shows a compact channel name with a clickable link
  • Much friendlier than seeing raw JSON parameters

4. New keep-coding-instructions Plugin Frontmatter Field

Section titled “4. New keep-coding-instructions Plugin Frontmatter Field”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Plugin output styles could override coding instructions from your configuration. The new field lets plugins declare “keep existing coding instructions.”

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • A code style plugin injects formatting rules
  • With keep-coding-instructions: true, your existing rules won’t be overwritten
  • Prevents plugin conflicts from losing coding style instructions

5. Hook Support for Setting Session Titles

Section titled “5. Hook Support for Setting Session Titles”

Background

Section titled “Background”

The UserPromptSubmit hook can now control session titles via hookSpecificOutput.sessionTitle.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Enterprise deployments: hooks automatically set titles matching ticket numbers

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.85: Introduced conditional if field for hooks
  • 2.1.84: Added TaskCreated hook
  • 2.1.78: Added StopFailure hook

6. Plugin Skills Now Use Frontmatter Name Instead of Directory Name

Section titled “6. Plugin Skills Now Use Frontmatter Name Instead of Directory Name”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When plugins declare skills with "skills": ["./"], the invocation name was previously derived from the directory name. Different installation methods could produce different directory names, causing unstable identifiers.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Plugin frontmatter declares name: lint-check
  • Before: Different names depending on installation method
  • Now: Always uses the frontmatter-defined name regardless of installation

7. Fixed Agents Appearing Stuck After Long Retry-After 429 Responses

Section titled “7. Fixed Agents Appearing Stuck After Long Retry-After 429 Responses”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When the API returned 429 with a long Retry-After (e.g., 300 seconds), Claude Code would silently wait with no feedback, making agents appear frozen.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • Running many parallel sub-agents in an enterprise environment
  • An agent hits rate limits with a “retry in 5 minutes” response
  • Before: Agent appears frozen for 5 minutes
  • Now: Error surfaces immediately; user decides to wait or cancel

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.90: Fixed rate limit dialog infinite loop causing session crashes
  • 2.1.89: Fixed autocompact death loop on repeated context overflow
  • 2.1.79: Fixed enterprise users unable to retry after 429 errors

8. Fixed macOS Keychain Lock Causing Silent Login Failure

Section titled “8. Fixed macOS Keychain Lock Causing Silent Login Failure”

Background

Section titled “Background”

macOS stores OAuth credentials in Keychain. After system restarts, a locked keychain caused Claude Code to show only “Not logged in” with no diagnostic info.

Use Cases

Section titled “Use Cases”
  • After macOS update and restart, Claude Code shows “Not logged in”
  • Now: Shows specific reason and claude doctor can diagnose and guide repair

9. Fixed Plugin Skill YAML Frontmatter Hooks Being Silently Ignored

Section titled “9. Fixed Plugin Skill YAML Frontmatter Hooks Being Silently Ignored”

A parsing bug caused hooks defined in plugin skill YAML frontmatter to be completely ignored without any warning. Now they’re correctly parsed and executed.

10. Fixed Plugin Hook Errors When Plugin Root Variable Was Not Set

Section titled “10. Fixed Plugin Hook Errors When Plugin Root Variable Was Not Set”

Plugin hooks referencing scripts via the plugin root path variable would fail with “No such file or directory” when the variable was unset. Now falls back to a reasonable default path.

11. Fixed Plugin Root Resolving to Marketplace Source Instead of Install Cache

Section titled “11. Fixed Plugin Root Resolving to Marketplace Source Instead of Install Cache”

For local-marketplace installed plugins, the root path variable incorrectly pointed to the original source directory rather than the installed cache. Only affects local-marketplace installations.

12. Fixed Repeated Diffs and Blank Pages in Long Session Scrollback

Section titled “12. Fixed Repeated Diffs and Blank Pages in Long Session Scrollback”

Long-running sessions with heavy diff output showed duplicate diffs and blank pages in the scrollback buffer.

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.92: Fixed same message appearing in two positions during fullscreen scrolling
  • 2.1.89: Added flicker-free rendering mode
  • 2.1.85: Improved scrolling performance for large transcripts

13. Fixed Multiline Prompt Indentation Alignment

Section titled “13. Fixed Multiline Prompt Indentation Alignment”

Wrapped lines in multiline prompts were incorrectly indented under the ❯ caret instead of under the text content.

14. Fixed Shift+Space Inserting Literal “space” in Search Inputs

Section titled “14. Fixed Shift+Space Inserting Literal “space” in Search Inputs”

A keyboard event handling bug caused Shift+Space to insert the literal string “space” instead of a space character.

15. Fixed Hyperlinks Opening Two Browser Tabs in tmux + xterm.js

Section titled “15. Fixed Hyperlinks Opening Two Browser Tabs in tmux + xterm.js”

OSC 8 hyperlink sequences were double-processed when tmux ran inside xterm.js terminals (VS Code Terminal, Hyper, Tabby). Only affects the tmux + xterm.js combination.

16. Fixed Ghost Lines Accumulating During Alt-Screen Scrolling

Section titled “16. Fixed Ghost Lines Accumulating During Alt-Screen Scrolling”

Content height changes mid-scroll left un-cleared old lines that compounded over time, requiring Ctrl+L to refresh.

17. Fixed FORCE_HYPERLINK Environment Variable Ignored in settings.json

Section titled “17. Fixed FORCE_HYPERLINK Environment Variable Ignored in settings.json”

Hyperlink detection occurred before settings loaded, so the variable set via settings.json was ignored. Now settings environment variables load before detection.

18. Fixed Native Cursor Not Tracking Tab Selection in Dialogs (Accessibility)

Section titled “18. Fixed Native Cursor Not Tracking Tab Selection in Dialogs (Accessibility)”

The terminal’s native cursor didn’t follow tab selection in dialogs, affecting screen reader and magnifier users.

19. Fixed Bedrock Invocation of Sonnet 3.5 v2 Model ID

Section titled “19. Fixed Bedrock Invocation of Sonnet 3.5 v2 Model ID”

Sonnet 3.5 v2 uses a new us. prefixed inference profile ID that Claude Code wasn’t using. Only affects Bedrock users.

20. Fixed SDK/Print Mode Losing Partial Responses on Interruption

Section titled “20. Fixed SDK/Print Mode Losing Partial Responses on Interruption”

In claude -p mode, interrupting mid-stream now preserves the partial response in conversation history for --resume. Particularly important for CI/CD pipelines.

21. Improved Cross-Worktree Session Resume

Section titled “21. Improved Cross-Worktree Session Resume”

Previously, --resume for sessions from a different Git worktree only printed a cd command. Now it directly resumes with automatic context switching.

22. Fixed CJK and Multibyte Text Corruption in stream-json

Section titled “22. Fixed CJK and Multibyte Text Corruption in stream-json”

UTF-8 CJK characters split at chunk boundaries were decoded as U+FFFD replacement characters. Affects all stream-json usage (SDK, piped output).

Version History

Section titled “Version History”
  • 2.1.89: Fixed CJK/emoji dropped at 4KB boundaries in prompt history
  • 2.1.77: Fixed CJK characters visually overflowing at UI right edge

Product Comparison

Section titled “Product Comparison”
  • Claude Code: Continuous CJK fixes indicate a large Asian user base
  • Codex CLI: No similar CJK fix records
  • Gemini CLI: Some unicode crash fixes, but less frequent

23. [VS Code] Reduced Cold-Start Subprocess Overhead

Section titled “23. [VS Code] Reduced Cold-Start Subprocess Overhead”

Session startup now parallelizes or eliminates unnecessary subprocess initialization, reducing cold-open time.

24. [VS Code] Fixed Dropdown Menu Mouse/Keyboard Selection Conflict

Section titled “24. [VS Code] Fixed Dropdown Menu Mouse/Keyboard Selection Conflict”

Mouse hover events overrode keyboard selection when the cursor was over the dropdown list, causing wrong item selection.

25. [VS Code] Added Warning Banner for Unparseable settings.json

Section titled “25. [VS Code] Added Warning Banner for Unparseable settings.json”

When settings.json has JSON syntax errors, Claude Code previously fell back silently to defaults — potentially disabling permission rules (security concern). Now shows a clear warning banner.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Release Characteristics

Section titled “Release Characteristics”

2.1.94 is primarily a stability and polish release. Among 28 changes:

  • New features: 4 (Mantle, effort defaults, Slack UI, plugin frontmatter)
  • Plugin/Hook system fixes: 5 (reflecting edge cases from rapid plugin ecosystem growth)
  • Terminal rendering fixes: 6 (scrollback, ghost lines, hyperlinks, CJK, etc.)
  • Platform compatibility: 3 (Bedrock, macOS keychain, tmux)
  • VS Code extension: 3
  • Other fixes: 7

Three-Product Comparison

Section titled “Three-Product Comparison”
  • Maturity: Claude Code is most mature (2.1.94 is extremely detailed); Codex CLI is newer; Gemini CLI is rapidly iterating
  • Plugin ecosystem: Claude Code is most complex (marketplace, hooks, skills); Codex CLI is simpler; Gemini CLI has an active extensions ecosystem
  • Terminal UI: Claude Code is highly complex (alt-screen, vim mode, voice); Codex CLI is minimal; Gemini CLI is catching up
  • Enterprise support: Claude Code is strongest (managed settings, multi-cloud); Codex CLI is OpenAI API only; Gemini CLI has Google Cloud + Vertex AI
  • CJK support: Claude Code invests heavily in fixes; others less so
  • Accessibility: Claude Code has screen reader/magnifier fix records; others don’t

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  1. Plugin system stabilization: Five plugin bug fixes indicate a shift from rapid iteration to stability
  2. Continued terminal rendering polish: Claude Code’s TUI complexity far exceeds competitors
  3. Multi-cloud inference: Mantle signals deeper infrastructure investment
  4. CJK/Internationalization: Continuous fixes across versions point to Asian market as a key growth area
  5. SDK/Automation: UTF-8 stream fixes and partial response preservation reflect growing CI/CD pipeline usage

  • Claude Code
  • AI Coding

Claude Code v2.1.90 Deep Dive: 19 Changes Dissected

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

1. Added /powerup — Interactive Tutorial System

Section titled “1. Added /powerup — Interactive Tutorial System”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code’s feature set has grown complex (hooks, MCP, plugins, agents, skills, auto mode, etc.), creating a steep learning curve for newcomers while even experienced users may not know all capabilities. The lack of in-product guidance has been consistent community feedback.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”
  • New users run /powerup after first install, learning core features like !bash mode, @ file references, /compact, and auto mode through animated demos
  • Team onboarding as a standard training step
  • Experienced users discovering hidden features (hooks, worktrees)

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Interactive tutorial, not a docs replacement; deep configuration still requires code.claude.com/docs
  • Animated demos depend on terminal rendering; minimal terminals (colorless SSH) may have degraded experience

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: /buddy April Fools’ Easter egg (hatching a creature that watches you code) — continuation of in-product fun
  • v2.1.84: New idle-return prompt guiding inactive users to /clear
  • Earlier: /tips briefly existed then was removed

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
Claude Code /powerupCodex CLIGemini CLI
In-product tutorial✅ Interactive animated lessons❌ None, relies on external docs❌ None, relies on codelabs
External tutorialsdocs + changelogdevelopers.openai.comcodelabs.developers.google.com

Codex CLI takes a minimalist approach with virtually no in-product guidance. Gemini CLI offers hands-on tutorials via Google Codelabs but not embedded. Claude Code’s /powerup is the only “in-product interactive tutorial” among the three.

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Expect adaptive recommendations based on user usage patterns
  • May evolve into a skill-based advanced curriculum (hooks development, plugin creation, etc.)

2. Added CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_KEEP_MARKETPLACE_ON_FAILURE Environment Variable

Section titled “2. Added CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_KEEP_MARKETPLACE_ON_FAILURE Environment Variable”

Background

Section titled “Background”

The plugin marketplace mechanism pulls the plugin index via git pull. In enterprise intranets/offline/unstable network environments, git pull failures clear the marketplace cache, losing installed plugin metadata.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Only preserves cache; plugins won’t auto-update — manual sync needed when network is available
  • Best used with CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR (pre-provisioning plugins offline)

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.83: Plugins load from disk cache, no longer re-pulled each time
  • v2.1.81: --bare skips plugin sync
  • v2.1.86: Marketplace script permission fix

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: No plugin ecosystem, this problem doesn’t exist
  • Gemini CLI: Extensions installed via npm/GitHub, no centralized marketplace; offline issues handled per-extension

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • With growing enterprise deployments, expect private marketplace mirror functionality
  • May support CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_MARKETPLACE_URL pointing to internal Git repos

3. Added .husky to Protected Directories (acceptEdits mode)

Section titled “3. Added .husky to Protected Directories (acceptEdits mode)”

Background

Section titled “Background”

.husky/ stores Git hooks (pre-commit, pre-push, etc.). If AI modifies these scripts freely, it could:

  • Bypass security policies (skipping lint, secret scanning)
  • Cause CI/CD pipeline anomalies
  • Inject malicious code into commit flows

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

In acceptEdits mode (auto-accept file edits), Claude attempting to modify .husky/pre-commit is blocked and prompts for confirmation, preventing accidental breakage of team Git hooks configuration.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Only effective in acceptEdits mode; normal mode already has permission confirmation
  • Protection list also includes .git, .claude, etc.

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.78: Fixed .git, .claude and other protected directories being writable in bypassPermissions mode
  • v2.1.85: Added conditional if field for hooks filtering

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Uses sandbox mode (network isolation + filesystem isolation), architecturally preventing such issues
  • Gemini CLI: Has accept-edits/yolo mode but no specific directory protection list

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Protection list will continue expanding (.github/workflows, Makefile, CI configs, and other sensitive files)
  • May evolve into user-configurable protectedPaths setting

4. Fixed Rate-limit Options Dialog Infinite Loop

Section titled “4. Fixed Rate-limit Options Dialog Infinite Loop”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When users hit API usage limits, Claude Code pops up an options dialog (wait/switch model/exit). A bug caused the dialog to immediately reappear after closing, forming an infinite loop that eventually consumed all memory and crashed the session.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”
  • Pro users hitting 5-hour rolling window limits during intensive coding
  • Dialog endlessly popping up → closing → popping up, terminal completely frozen, can only kill the process

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • If still encountering similar issues, use Ctrl+C to force interrupt or kill the process
  • Combined with v2.1.80’s rate_limits statusline field, users can anticipate approaching limits

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Fixed misleading “Rate limit reached” message (actually entitlement error)
  • v2.1.80: Statusline added rate limit usage display
  • v2.1.79: Fixed enterprise users unable to retry on 429 errors

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Silently waits or errors out on rate limits, no interactive dialog
  • Gemini CLI: v0.4.0 introduced Pro Quota Dialog allowing auth method switching or model downgrade

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Expect automatic downgrade strategies (auto-switching to lower-cost models)
  • May support queueing and automatic recovery when limits reset

5. Fixed --resume Prompt-cache Miss (Regression Since v2.1.69)

Section titled “5. Fixed --resume Prompt-cache Miss (Regression Since v2.1.69)”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When resuming sessions with --resume, the first API request completely missed prompt cache, causing all context to be recomputed (full cache invalidation). For users with deferred tools, MCP servers, or custom agents, this was extremely costly — 2-10x more token spending. This was a regression introduced in v2.1.69.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Prompt cache savings are real money (cache hit pricing is only 1/10th)
  • Especially critical for long session resumes; ensure upgrade to 2.1.90+

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Fixed prompt cache miss in long sessions (tool schema byte changes)
  • v2.1.86: Fixed prompt cache hit rate issues (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry)
  • v2.1.77: Fixed --resume race condition truncating session history
  • v2.1.69: Version that introduced this regression

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Each run is independent, no session resume concept, no cache reuse
  • Gemini CLI: No explicit session resume; exports sessions via /chat share but doesn’t support restore

Claude Code’s session resume + prompt caching is one of its unique competitive advantages.

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Prompt caching is Anthropic’s core differentiator; expect continued cache hit rate optimization
  • May introduce persistent cache (cross-session partial cache reuse)

6. Fixed Edit/Write “File content has changed” with Format-on-save Hooks

Section titled “6. Fixed Edit/Write “File content has changed” with Format-on-save Hooks”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Users configured PostToolUse hooks for format-on-save (prettier, black, etc.). When Claude executed two consecutive Edits, the first Edit triggered the hook which formatted file content, and the second Edit found file content didn’t match expectations (modified by hook), erroring with “File content has changed.”

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Editing two functions consecutively: first edit → prettier formats → second edit detects file changed → error interruption.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • After fix, Claude re-reads file content after hook execution before next edit
  • Still recommended to avoid hooks doing overly aggressive rewrites (changing line count structure)

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Bash tool added warning when formatter/linter modifies previously read files
  • v2.1.85: Hooks added conditional if field to reduce unnecessary hook triggers

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Executes in sandbox, no hook system, this problem doesn’t exist
  • Gemini CLI: No PostToolUse hook mechanism; formatting relies on user or IDE config

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Hook system will mature; expect transactional guarantees for hook chains
  • May support hook diff feedback to AI, letting it perceive formatting changes

7. Fixed PreToolUse Hooks Exit Code 2 Not Blocking Tool Call

Section titled “7. Fixed PreToolUse Hooks Exit Code 2 Not Blocking Tool Call”

Background

Section titled “Background”

PreToolUse hooks are designed so exit code 2 = block tool call, with hooks providing rejection reasons via stdout JSON. A bug caused blocking logic to fail when hooks simultaneously output JSON to stdout and exited with code 2 — the tool still executed.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • This is a security-related fix — teams relying on hooks for access control must upgrade
  • v2.1.89 also fixed PreToolUse hooks returning “allow” bypassing deny rules

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Added defer permission decision, PermissionDenied hook
  • v2.1.85: PreToolUse hooks support updatedInput + allow
  • v2.1.84: Added TaskCreated hook
  • v2.1.77: Fixed PreToolUse hooks returning “allow” bypassing enterprise deny rules

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: No hook system; permissions entirely via sandbox + approval modes
  • Gemini CLI: No equivalent PreToolUse hooks; security via modes (shell/accept-edits/yolo)

Claude Code’s hook system is the most complex and flexible enterprise capability among the three.

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Hook system is becoming Claude Code’s enterprise security cornerstone
  • Expect type-safe schema validation and testing frameworks for hooks

8. Fixed Collapsed Search/Read Summary Badge Appearing Multiple Times

Section titled “8. Fixed Collapsed Search/Read Summary Badge Appearing Multiple Times”

Background

Section titled “Background”

During fullscreen scroll-back, if CLAUDE.md files auto-loaded during tool calls, collapsed search/read summary badges would appear multiple times, cluttering the interface.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Pure UI issue, doesn’t affect functionality
  • v2.1.89 also fixed similar badge duplication during parallel tool use

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Fixed nested CLAUDE.md being injected dozens of times in long sessions
  • v2.1.89: Fixed badge duplication during parallel tool use
  • v2.1.83: Fixed scrollback jumping from tool group collapsing

9. Fixed Auto Mode Not Respecting Explicit User Boundaries

Section titled “9. Fixed Auto Mode Not Respecting Explicit User Boundaries”

Background

Section titled “Background”

In auto mode, Claude executes operations without per-action confirmation. But when users explicitly stated “don’t push” or “wait for X before Y,” auto mode’s classifier ignored these natural language constraints and still executed prohibited operations.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • This is a critical trust and safety fix — auto mode reliability directly determines user adoption
  • After fix, auto mode classifier parses negative/conditional instructions from user messages

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Auto mode rejected commands now show notification and can be retried in /permissions
  • v2.1.80: Auto mode shows “unavailable for your plan” when plan-restricted
  • v2.1.76: Auto-compaction circuit breaker after consecutive failures

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Three modes (suggest/auto-edit/full-auto), full-auto has sandbox protection but no natural language boundary parsing
  • Gemini CLI: Yolo mode fully automatic, no natural language constraint parsing

Claude Code leads here — attempting to understand and respect natural language boundaries is a more advanced AI safety strategy.

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Auto mode classifier will continue improving; expect structured boundary declarations (--no-push, --dry-run semantic flags)
  • May develop into “constrained auto mode” with user-predefined allowed/forbidden operation sets

10. Fixed Click-to-expand Hover Text Invisible on Light Themes

Section titled “10. Fixed Click-to-expand Hover Text Invisible on Light Themes”

Background

Section titled “Background”

On light terminal themes, hover text color was too close to background color, making it nearly invisible.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Benefits users on light themes (e.g., Solarized Light)
  • Dark themes unaffected

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.78: Fixed Claude orange being too faint in VS Code/Cursor terminals

11. Fixed UI Crash on Malformed Tool Input in Permission Dialog

Section titled “11. Fixed UI Crash on Malformed Tool Input in Permission Dialog”

Background

Section titled “Background”

When MCP servers or models returned malformed tool input, the permission confirmation dialog attempted to render it, crashing the entire UI.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Defensive fix improving robustness
  • More likely triggered by third-party MCP servers

12. Fixed Headers Disappearing When Scrolling Selection Screens

Section titled “12. Fixed Headers Disappearing When Scrolling Selection Screens”

Background

Section titled “Background”

/model, /config and other selection screens lost their headers when scrolling, removing navigation reference points.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Pure UI polish
  • More reproducible with fewer terminal rows

13. Hardened PowerShell Tool Permission Checks

Section titled “13. Hardened PowerShell Tool Permission Checks”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Windows PowerShell tool permission checks had multiple security vulnerabilities:

  1. Trailing & bypass: Appending & to create background jobs bypassed permission checks
  2. -ErrorAction Break hang: Triggered debugger causing session hang
  3. Archive-extraction TOCTOU: Time-of-Check-Time-of-Use race condition during file extraction
  4. Parse-fail fallback degradation: Deny rules degraded when command parsing failed

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Windows users strongly recommended to upgrade
  • PowerShell tool introduced as opt-in preview in v2.1.84; security hardening is rapidly iterating

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: PowerShell 5.1 double-quote + space argument hardening
  • v2.1.85: PowerShell dangerous command detection improvements
  • v2.1.84: First introduction of PowerShell tool (opt-in preview)

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Uses Linux sandbox (macOS uses Apple Seatbelt), doesn’t support PowerShell
  • Gemini CLI: Shell tool supports Windows but lacks equivalent fine-grained command parsing security layer

Claude Code’s PowerShell security investment is deepest among the three, but this also reflects the larger attack surface of a non-sandbox architecture.

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • PowerShell tool will transition from opt-in preview to default-on
  • Expect Windows sandbox support (possibly based on Windows Sandbox or Hyper-V)

14. Improved Performance: Eliminated Per-turn JSON.stringify of MCP Tool Schemas

Section titled “14. Improved Performance: Eliminated Per-turn JSON.stringify of MCP Tool Schemas”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Every AI turn ran JSON.stringify on MCP tool schemas to compute cache keys. With many MCP tools (enterprise environments may have 50+), this caused unnecessary CPU and memory overhead.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Configured with multiple MCP servers (Slack, Gmail, GitHub, DB, etc.), each exposing 5-20 tools, serializing all schemas every turn caused noticeable latency.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Minimal impact for users with few tools
  • Heavy MCP users (enterprise scenarios) benefit most

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Fixed prompt cache miss from tool schema byte changes
  • v2.1.84: MCP tool descriptions truncated to 2KB to prevent context bloat

15. Improved Performance: SSE Transport Linear Time (Was Quadratic)

Section titled “15. Improved Performance: SSE Transport Linear Time (Was Quadratic)”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Server-Sent Events transport processing of large streaming frames had O(n²) complexity (likely string concatenation or repeated scanning), causing severe latency in large responses.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”
  • Generating long code files (thousands of lines) with progressively slowing stream rendering
  • Especially noticeable with Opus model generating long reasoning outputs

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Classic “progressive performance degradation” — invisible for short responses, exponential worsening for long ones

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Uses OpenAI’s Responses API with different streaming implementation
  • Gemini CLI: Based on gRPC/REST streaming with its own optimization path

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Streaming rendering performance will continue improving; may introduce incremental parsing

16. Improved Performance: SDK Sessions Quadratic Transcript Writes → Linear

Section titled “16. Improved Performance: SDK Sessions Quadratic Transcript Writes → Linear”

Background

Section titled “Background”

In long SDK sessions, transcript write time grew quadratically with session length. 50MB+ session files could take seconds to write.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”
  • Integrating Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines via SDK for long-running tasks
  • Extended pair programming sessions (hours, hundreds of tool calls)

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.89: Fixed >50MB session file crashes
  • v2.1.83: Reduced long-session scrollback reset frequency
  • v2.1.77: Improved --resume memory usage for large sessions

17. Improved /resume Parallel Loading for All-projects View

Section titled “17. Improved /resume Parallel Loading for All-projects View”

Background

Section titled “Background”

/resume’s “all projects” view loaded each project’s session list serially. With many projects, wait time was excessive.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

Developers working across 10+ projects: /resume originally needed 5-10 seconds to load all project sessions; parallelization reduced this to 1-2 seconds.

Related Changes

Section titled “Related Changes”
  • v2.1.77: --resume large session loading 45% faster, 100-150MB less memory

18. Changed --resume Picker to Exclude claude -p / SDK Sessions

Section titled “18. Changed --resume Picker to Exclude claude -p / SDK Sessions”

Background

Section titled “Background”

claude -p (print mode / non-interactive) and SDK sessions aren’t suitable for interactive resume — they’re typically one-shot script calls. Including them in the picker cluttered the list when users looked for actual interactive sessions to restore.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • These sessions still exist on disk; just not shown in the picker
  • To resume specific SDK sessions, use --resume <session-id> directly

19. Removed DNS Cache Commands from Auto-allow

Section titled “19. Removed DNS Cache Commands from Auto-allow”

Background

Section titled “Background”

Get-DnsClientCache (PowerShell) and ipconfig /displaydns (cmd) can expose complete DNS query history — essentially a proxy for browsing history. Auto-allowing these commands posed privacy risks.

Use Cases & Examples

Section titled “Use Cases & Examples”

In auto mode, if Claude ran Get-DnsClientCache for debugging purposes, it would obtain the user’s complete list of visited domains, including potentially sensitive browsing behavior.

Notes

Section titled “Notes”
  • Only affects Windows users
  • Removing auto-allow means these commands can still execute but require manual user confirmation

Competitor Comparison

Section titled “Competitor Comparison”
  • Codex CLI: Sandbox prohibits network access by default; DNS cache viewing is meaningless
  • Gemini CLI: No equivalent fine-grained command allowlist management

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  • Privacy protection granularity is an inevitable trend for AI tools
  • Expect a privacy impact classification system — categorizing commands by data sensitivity

Summary: Version Positioning & Overall Trends

Section titled “Summary: Version Positioning & Overall Trends”

v2.1.90 Classification

Section titled “v2.1.90 Classification”

This is a stability, security, and performance-focused release. Among 19 changes:

  • 3 new features (/powerup, env var, protected dir)
  • 10 bug fixes (3 security-related)
  • 3 performance optimizations (all complexity downgrades)
  • 3 improvements/changes

Three-product Evolution Comparison

Section titled “Three-product Evolution Comparison”
DimensionClaude CodeCodex CLIGemini CLI
ArchitectureNo sandbox + permission system + hooksSandbox-firstMode switching (shell/yolo)
Security StrategyDefense in depth (hooks + rules + auto mode classifier)Isolation defense (sandbox)Lightweight defense
Session ManagementResume + cache + long session optimizationStatelessBasic history
Extension EcosystemPlugins + MCP + hooks + skillsMCP (basic)Extensions + MCP
Enterprise Capabilitiesmanaged-settings + permission policies + OTelBasicCode Assist integration
Release Cadence~Every 2 days~Monthly~Weekly

Claude Code is becoming the most complex terminal AI coding tool, with its hooks/plugin/MCP three-layer extension system and enterprise security capabilities far exceeding competitors. However, complexity also brings higher bug density and maintenance burden (v2.1.89 alone had 40+ fixes). Codex CLI takes the simplicity route with sandbox security at its core. Gemini CLI falls between the two, emphasizing Google Cloud ecosystem integration.

Claude Code v2.1.86 Deep Dive: All 28 Changes Explained

Mar 31, 2026
Vibe Sparking

This is a stability and polish-focused release with 28 changes: 1 new feature, 2 optimizations, and 25 fixes/improvements. Here’s the full breakdown.

I. New Features

Section titled “I. New Features”

1. X-Claude-Code-Session-Id HTTP Header

Section titled “1. X-Claude-Code-Session-Id HTTP Header”

Background: Enterprises using API proxies/gateways (LiteLLM, Helicone, Portkey) for cost tracking and rate limiting need to know “which requests belong to the same Claude Code session.” Previously, this required parsing the JSON body’s conversation metadata — fragile and a privacy risk.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise IT aggregates per-developer, per-session token consumption via proxy
  • Security auditing: tracking abnormally high-frequency sessions
  • Example: X-Claude-Code-Session-Id: sess_abc123 → proxy buckets by header directly, no body parsing needed

Notes:

  • Session IDs can be correlated to user behavior; proxy logs need proper anonymization
  • Self-hosted proxies must pass this header through — don’t let WAF rules strip it

Competitive comparison:

ProductSession Tracking
Claude CodeDedicated HTTP header (new)
CursorBuilt-in dashboard, no session-level header
Continue.devNo native solution, requires custom injection
CopilotGitHub backend stats, no proxy-level granularity

Trend: As AI coding agents enter enterprises, observability becomes table stakes. Expect dedicated AI agent APM toolchains (think Datadog for AI agents).

2. .jj / .sl Added to VCS Exclusion List

Section titled “2. .jj / .sl Added to VCS Exclusion List”

Background: Jujutsu (.jj/) and Sapling (.sl/) are next-gen version control systems. Previously, Claude Code’s grep and file completion would dive into these directories, surfacing metadata noise.

Use cases:

  • Teams using Jujutsu for monorepos — @ file completion no longer shows .jj/store/ object files
  • Code search no longer hits .sl/ internal state

Competitive comparison:

  • VS Code: .gitignore-driven, requires manual .jj addition
  • Cursor: No explicit Jujutsu/Sapling exclusion yet
  • JetBrains: Has Jujutsu plugin, but index exclusion needs configuration

Trend: Jujutsu is growing rapidly (already used at scale inside Google). Expect native support across IDEs and AI coding tools by late 2026.

II. Core Bug Fixes

Section titled “II. Core Bug Fixes”

3. --resume Throws “tool_use ids without tool_result blocks”

Section titled “3. --resume Throws “tool_use ids without tool_result blocks””

Background: v2.1.85 changed session serialization format, causing old session restores to have tool_use blocks without matching tool_result — API validation failure. A version compatibility break.

Scenario: Developer creates a long session in v2.1.84, upgrades, uses claude --resume → immediate crash.

Competitive comparison: Cursor and Copilot Chat sessions are short-lived — cross-version resume barely exists. Claude Code’s --resume is a differentiator but carries maintenance burden.

Trend: Agent session resume will become critical. Expect standardized agent conversation serialization formats.

4. Write/Edit/Read Fail on Files Outside Project Root

Section titled “4. Write/Edit/Read Fail on Files Outside Project Root”

Background: When conditional skills or rules are configured, file operations on paths like ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md fail. The conditional skill path validation was too strict, confining all paths to the project root.

Scenario: User maintains global instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md → Agent tries to read/edit → blocked by conditional skill sandbox logic.

Competitive comparison:

  • Cursor: Rules files are project-only — no global rules capability, no issue
  • Windsurf: Similar global + project-level config layering
  • Copilot: Fixed instruction file location, unconditional loading

Trend: AI coding agent permission models will increasingly resemble OS file permissions — allow-lists + layered policies.

5. Every Skill Call Triggers Unnecessary Config Disk Write

Section titled “5. Every Skill Call Triggers Unnecessary Config Disk Write”

Background: Each skill invocation wrote the config file to disk. Especially severe on Windows — NTFS handles frequent small writes poorly, and concurrent writes can corrupt the config.

Scenario: Heavy skill users on Windows find Claude Code getting progressively slower. Worst case: config file corrupted by concurrent writes.

Competitive comparison: Most competitors use in-memory cache + debounced writes. This is an engineering maturity gap for Claude Code.

6. /feedback OOM Crash on Ultra-Long Sessions

Section titled “6. /feedback OOM Crash on Ultra-Long Sessions”

Background: /feedback serializes the entire conversation transcript. Sessions with thousands of turns can produce transcripts of hundreds of MB, causing Node.js heap overflow.

Scenario: Developer works an 8-hour marathon session, tries to submit feedback → process killed.

Competitive comparison:

  • Cursor: Each Composer interaction is independent — no ultra-long sessions
  • Copilot Chat: Implicit session length limits

Trend: Agent “session lifecycle management” will become a product design focus — session pruning, archival, and summarization.

7. --bare Mode Missing MCP Tools + Silently Dropping Messages

Section titled “7. --bare Mode Missing MCP Tools + Silently Dropping Messages”

Background: --bare mode (minimal UI for embedding) had two independent bugs:

  1. MCP tools weren’t injected into the tool list
  2. Messages enqueued mid-turn were silently dropped

Scenario: Embedding Claude Code via --bare in a custom IDE → MCP tools (DB queries, etc.) unavailable. Sending concurrent messages → messages lost without error.

Trend: Claude Code is evolving from “terminal tool” to “embeddable agent runtime.” --bare mode quality directly determines ecosystem ceiling.

III. Terminal UI Fixes

Section titled “III. Terminal UI Fixes”

8-12: Precision Terminal Experience Fixes

Section titled “8-12: Precision Terminal Experience Fixes”
BugRoot CauseImpact
c hotkey only copies ~20 chars of OAuth URLClipboard write length truncationCan’t complete OAuth login
OAuth password input leaks token prefix on narrow terminalsMasked input line-wrap exposes plaintextSecurity issue ⚠️
Plugin script Permission denied (macOS/Linux)v2.1.83 regression, +x not set on filesAll marketplace plugins broken
Statusline shows other instance’s model nameRace condition in shared multi-instance stateUser misjudges current model
Scroll doesn’t follow new messagesScroll lock state not properly resetMust manually scroll to bottom

OAuth token leak (item 9) deserves special attention — a real security vulnerability. In narrow terminals (e.g., split tmux panes), pasting an OAuth code with masked input’s line-wrap logic exposes the first few characters. While insufficient alone for an attack, it’s a risk in shoulder-surfing or screen-recording scenarios.

13-16: Interaction Detail Fixes

Section titled “13-16: Interaction Detail Fixes”
BugDescription
/plugin uninstall n key behaves counterintuitivelyPressing n should mean “don’t keep data” → actually became the uninstall trigger
Blank transcript after pressing EnterRace condition, UI not rendered before response arrives
Ultrathink hint persists after keyword deletionIncomplete state cleanup
Markdown/highlight render cache memory leakLong sessions: cache holds full content strings without releasing

Memory leak (item 16) explains why long-running Claude Code sessions get progressively slower — the markdown renderer’s cache keeps growing.

IV. Performance Optimizations

Section titled “IV. Performance Optimizations”

17. macOS Keychain Cache: 5s → 30s

Section titled “17. macOS Keychain Cache: 5s → 30s”

Background: Each claude.ai MCP connector startup queries macOS Keychain for tokens. With multiple MCPs configured, Keychain calls block the event loop serially, causing startup lag.

Scenario: 5+ MCP connectors configured (GitHub, Jira, Slack, DB, custom) → startup takes several seconds.

Optimization: Cache window expanded from 5s to 30s — multiple connectors share a single keychain query.

18. @ File References No Longer JSON-Escape Raw Content

Section titled “18. @ File References No Longer JSON-Escape Raw Content”

Background: Using @filename to reference files caused content to be JSON string-escaped (\n → \\n, " → \"), needlessly inflating token count.

Scenario: Referencing a 1000-line JSON file → escape overhead adds 10-20% more tokens.

Optimization: Raw strings passed directly — saves tokens, saves money.

19. Read Tool: Compact Line Numbers + Deduplicated Unchanged Reads

Section titled “19. Read Tool: Compact Line Numbers + Deduplicated Unchanged Reads”

Background: Read tool previously returned full content every time, even when unchanged. Line number formatting was also verbose.

Combined impact of items 17-19: For heavy users, these three optimizations can save 5-15% token usage per session — direct cost savings.

20. Improved Prompt Cache Hit Rate for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry

Section titled “20. Improved Prompt Cache Hit Rate for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry”

Background: Tool descriptions contained dynamic content (timestamps), causing prompt prefix to differ per request → cache miss.

Optimization: Removing dynamic content makes tool descriptions static → stable prompt prefix → cache hits.

Competitive comparison: This leverages Anthropic’s unique prompt caching. OpenAI’s prefix caching has similar optimization potential, but Cursor et al. don’t expose this level of control.

V. UX Improvements

Section titled “V. UX Improvements”

21-25: Quality of Life

Section titled “21-25: Quality of Life”
ImprovementDescription
Memory filenames now clickable/highlighted”Saved 3 memories” filenames become interactive links
/skills description truncated to 250 charsPrevents long skill descriptions from eating context
/skills sorted alphabeticallyFrom “random order” to “predictable order”
Auto mode shows reason when unavailableFrom vague “temporarily unavailable” to “your plan doesn’t support this”
[VSCode] Long operations no longer falsely report “Not responding”Timeout threshold raised or switched to heartbeat detection
[VSCode] Max plan users downgraded to Sonnet after 8hOAuth token refresh loses plan info

VSCode Sonnet downgrade (item 25) is particularly damaging — Max plan users paying top dollar get silently downgraded to Sonnet after 8 hours, with noticeably lower output quality and zero notification. This severely impacts user trust.

VI. Overall Assessment

Section titled “VI. Overall Assessment”

Release Positioning

Section titled “Release Positioning”

This is a textbook stabilization release with minimal new features, focused on:

  1. Reliability: Resume, OOM, config corruption fixes
  2. Security: OAuth token leak patch
  3. Performance: Token savings, faster startup, memory leak fix
  4. Enterprise readiness: Session ID header, Bedrock/Vertex cache optimization

Competitive Overview

Section titled “Competitive Overview”
DimensionClaude CodeCursorCopilotWindsurf
Terminal-native✅ Core strength❌❌❌
Session resume✅❌❌Partial
Enterprise proxy support✅ New headerDashboardGitHub backend❌
Plugin ecosystem🟡 Growing✅ Mature✅ Mature🟡
Stability🟡 Rapid iteration✅ Relatively stable✅ Stable🟡
VCS breadth✅ Git+Jujutsu+SaplingGit onlyGit onlyGit only

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  1. Agent Runtime Evolution: --bare fixes + Session ID header signal Claude Code evolving from CLI tool to embeddable agent runtime
  2. Enterprise Observability: Session tracking → future spans/traces → full AI agent observability
  3. Session Lifecycle Management: OOM fix is a band-aid; long-term needs session pruning, auto-summarization, segmented resume
  4. Multi-VCS World: Jujutsu support signals the post-Git era — dev tools need to be VCS-agnostic
  5. Token Economics: Three stacked token optimizations show Anthropic is serious about API cost optimization — key to retaining power users

Claude Code v2.1.87 ~ v2.1.88 Deep Dive

Mar 31, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis date: 2026-03-31 | Source: CHANGELOG.md

v2.1.87 is a single-line hotfix, while v2.1.88 is a major quality update — covering 3 new features, 40+ fixes, and several UX improvements. Both versions analyzed together.

0. v2.1.87: Cowork Dispatch Message Delivery Fix

Section titled “0. v2.1.87: Cowork Dispatch Message Delivery Fix”

Fixed messages in Cowork Dispatch not getting delivered

Section titled “Fixed messages in Cowork Dispatch not getting delivered”

Background: Cowork is Anthropic’s “AI collaboration desktop” feature launched in early 2026, allowing Claude to autonomously operate apps in a macOS sandbox. Dispatch is a Cowork sub-feature — users can remotely assign tasks from iPhone/iPad to a Mac Cowork session, like “remote-controlling your AI assistant.”

v2.1.87 fixes: instructions sent via Dispatch weren’t being delivered to the Cowork session, causing a silent failure of “sent but Claude never received it.”

Use case:

  • You’re commuting, open the Claude app on iPhone, and ask Cowork on your Mac to refactor a module
  • After sending, the Mac shows no response — this was the bug
  • After the fix, the mobile → Mac Dispatch message pipeline works again

Notes:

  • Dispatch is currently limited to Max subscribers (gradually rolling out to Pro)
  • Mac-side Cowork session must be active to receive messages
  • Messages are still lost if Mac is asleep or Cowork has exited

Competitive comparison:

ProductCross-device AI collaboration
Claude Code + DispatchMobile remote Cowork tasks, sandboxed execution
Codex (OpenAI)App-server mode with WebSocket remote connection, but no native mobile integration
Gemini CLINo cross-device collaboration, terminal-only
CursorNo remote dispatch capability

Trend: Cross-device AI agent collaboration is becoming a key differentiator. Anthropic pioneered the “phone → Mac AI desktop” loop through Cowork + Dispatch. Expect OpenAI to follow via Codex App + ChatGPT mobile.

1. New Features — v2.1.88

Section titled “1. New Features — v2.1.88”

1. CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1: Flicker-Free Rendering

Section titled “1. CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1: Flicker-Free Rendering”

Background: Claude Code’s streaming output causes visible flickering from frequent screen redraws, especially in iTerm2, Kitty, and tmux combinations. Users see text jumping and cursor drift during long sessions.

Technical approach: Enables alt-screen rendering with virtualized scrollback, batching redraws to eliminate per-line flicker.

Usage:

  • Ideal for long coding sessions and heavy parallel tool calls
  • Most noticeable improvement in tmux + iTerm2

Notes:

  • This is opt-in — Anthropic isn’t fully confident in stability yet
  • Alt-screen mode changes native terminal scroll behavior (uses virtualized scrollback)
  • Some terminals (e.g., older Terminal.app) may not be compatible
  • Test in non-critical sessions first

Competitive comparison:

ProductTerminal rendering strategy
Claude CodeOpt-in alt-screen + virtualized scrollback (new)
Codex CLIRust TUI (ratatui), native alt-screen, fewer flicker issues
Gemini CLIInk (React-based TUI), already uses alt-screen by default
AiderStandard stdout, simple but flicker-free

2. PermissionDenied Hook: Programmable Retry After Auto-Mode Rejection

Section titled “2. PermissionDenied Hook: Programmable Retry After Auto-Mode Rejection”

Background: Claude Code’s Auto mode has a built-in classifier that blocks commands it considers dangerous (like rm -rf, git push --force). But in some workflows, user-defined hooks can safely handle these operations (e.g., in CI/CD, git push is expected). Previously, blocked commands required manual confirmation with no programmatic entry point.

Usage:

Notes:

  • ⚠️ This is a “bypass safety” interface — ensure your retry logic is itself safe
  • {retry: true} tells the model “you may retry” — it doesn’t guarantee it will
  • Hooks have timeout limits
  • Best used alongside v2.1.85’s PreToolUse hook if condition filtering

Competitive comparison:

ProductProgrammable response to permission denial
Claude CodePermissionDenied hook → {retry: true} (new)
Codex CLIStatic sandbox policy, no dynamic hook mechanism
Gemini CLIPolicy engine with admin-policy flag, but no per-denial hook
CursorNo similar mechanism

Trend: AI coding agent permission models are evolving from “global switches” to “programmable policy engines.” Claude Code’s hook chain (PreToolUse → PostToolUse → PermissionDenied) is the most complete in the industry.

3. Named Subagents in @ Mention Autocomplete

Section titled “3. Named Subagents in @ Mention Autocomplete”

Background: Claude Code supports forking subagents for parallel task execution. Previously, users needed to remember subagent IDs — not intuitive.

Usage:

  • Fork a subagent named refactor-auth, then type @ref in the main session to autocomplete to @refactor-auth
  • Quickly reference and switch between different agents’ outputs in multi-agent scenarios

Competitive comparison:

ProductMulti-agent reference method
Claude Code@name autocomplete (new)
Codex CLIPath-style addresses like /root/agent_a (v0.117.0), structured messages
Gemini CLISubagents enabled by default, but no user-level naming/reference UI

Trend: Multi-agent collaboration is shifting from “system auto-orchestration” to “user-perceivable agent addressing.” A standardized agent addressing protocol may emerge.

2. Critical Fixes — v2.1.88

Section titled “2. Critical Fixes — v2.1.88”

4. Prompt Cache Miss Fix: The Hidden Cost Killer for Long Sessions

Section titled “4. Prompt Cache Miss Fix: The Hidden Cost Killer for Long Sessions”

Background: Anthropic’s API supports prompt caching — identical prefixes can reuse cache, reducing input token costs by 90%. But Claude Code’s tool schema byte count changes during sessions (e.g., MCP tools dynamically loading/unloading), causing cache key changes and frequent misses.

Impact: Long session costs could be 2-5x higher than expected.

5. Nested CLAUDE.md Duplicate Injection: Token Explosion in Long Sessions

Section titled “5. Nested CLAUDE.md Duplicate Injection: Token Explosion in Long Sessions”

Background: In long sessions, nested CLAUDE.md files were injected dozens of times, filling context with meaningless repetition.

Impact: Degraded model quality in later session stages; especially severe in monorepos with CLAUDE.md in each package.

Fix: Each CLAUDE.md is now injected exactly once.

6. Edit/Write Tool CRLF and Markdown Hard Break Issues on Windows

Section titled “6. Edit/Write Tool CRLF and Markdown Hard Break Issues on Windows”

Two related bugs:

  1. Windows CRLF (\r\n) doubled to \r\r\n, causing blank lines
  2. Markdown hard breaks (trailing two spaces) were incorrectly stripped

7. StructuredOutput Schema Cache Bug: ~50% Workflow Failure Rate

Section titled “7. StructuredOutput Schema Cache Bug: ~50% Workflow Failure Rate”

Background: When switching schemas within the same session, cache wasn’t properly invalidated — ~50% of requests used the wrong schema validation, returning 400 errors.

Impact: Severely affected automation workflow reliability.

8. Memory Leak: LRU Cache Keys Retaining Large JSON Inputs

Section titled “8. Memory Leak: LRU Cache Keys Retaining Large JSON Inputs”

Long-running sessions: large JSON inputs retained as LRU cache keys caused continuous memory growth, potentially reaching several GB.

9. Edit Tool OOM Crash on Files >1 GiB

Section titled “9. Edit Tool OOM Crash on Files >1 GiB”

Entire file loaded into memory for diff on oversized files. Now uses streaming or refuses the operation.

10. Misleading “Rate limit reached” Error Messages

Section titled “10. Misleading “Rate limit reached” Error Messages”

API entitlement errors (plan limitations, quota exhaustion) were all shown as “Rate limit reached.” Now displays actual error with actionable guidance.

11. LSP Server Zombie State Fix

Section titled “11. LSP Server Zombie State Fix”

LSP server crashes left a zombie state with silent failures for all language analysis features. Now auto-restarts on next request.

12. Hooks if Condition Filtering: Compound Commands and Env Prefixes

Section titled “12. Hooks if Condition Filtering: Compound Commands and Env Prefixes”

Bash(git push*) couldn’t match ls && git push or FOO=bar git push. Fixed.

13. CJK / Emoji History Entries Discarded at 4KB Boundary

Section titled “13. CJK / Emoji History Entries Discarded at 4KB Boundary”

UTF-8 multi-byte characters split at 4KB chunk boundaries caused CJK and emoji history entries to be silently dropped. Major impact for Chinese/Japanese/Korean users.

14. /stats Data Loss and Incomplete Statistics

Section titled “14. /stats Data Loss and Incomplete Statistics”
  1. Stats cache format changes caused loss of 30+ day history → now migrated
  2. Subagent and fork token usage now included in /stats

3. Terminal UI & Rendering Fixes — v2.1.88

Section titled “3. Terminal UI & Rendering Fixes — v2.1.88”
  • 15. Scroll-back disappearing in long sessions — fully fixed
  • 16. Duplicate collapse badges during parallel tool calls
  • 17. Notification invalidates not clearing current notification
  • 18. Input box briefly disappearing after prompt submission
  • 19. /btw long responses now use scrollable viewport
  • 20. Devanagari and combining mark text truncation — i18n fix
  • 21. Rendering artifacts after terminal layout changes

4. Voice Mode Fixes — v2.1.88

Section titled “4. Voice Mode Fixes — v2.1.88”
  • 22. macOS Apple Silicon microphone permission request failure
  • 23. Push-to-talk hotkey combinations not activating
  • 24. Windows WebSocket upgrade “HTTP 101” error

5. Windows / PowerShell Fixes — v2.1.88

Section titled “5. Windows / PowerShell Fixes — v2.1.88”
  • 25. Shift+Enter submitting instead of newline in Windows Terminal Preview 1.25
  • 26. Periodic UI jitter in iTerm2 + tmux during streaming
  • 27. PowerShell tool misreporting stderr as failure (e.g., git push progress output)
  • 28. PowerShell prompt now version-aware (5.1 vs 7+)

6. SDK / Automation Fixes — v2.1.88

Section titled “6. SDK / Automation Fixes — v2.1.88”
  • 29. SDK error results now correctly set is_error: true
  • 30. Task notification lost when backgrounding sessions with Ctrl+B
  • 31. PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks file_path now uses absolute paths

7. UX Improvements — v2.1.88

Section titled “7. UX Improvements — v2.1.88”
  • 32. Thinking summaries hidden by default (set showThinkingSummaries: true to restore)
  • 33. Auto-mode denied commands now show notifications + visible in /permissions
  • 34. /env now applies to PowerShell tool
  • 35. /usage hides redundant info for Pro/Enterprise users
  • 36. Collapsed tool summaries: ls/tree/du now show “Listed N directories”
  • 37. Image paste no longer inserts trailing space
  • 38. Pasting !command now enters bash mode

8. Comprehensive Comparison: Claude Code vs Codex CLI vs Gemini CLI (March 2026)

9. Future Trends

1. Multi-Agent Collaboration as Core Competitive Advantage

Section titled “1. Multi-Agent Collaboration as Core Competitive Advantage”

All three invested heavily in multi-agent architecture in 2026 Q1. Expect cross-tool agent communication standards by H2 2026.

2. Cross-Device AI Development: From “Works” to “Works Well”

Cowork Dispatch and Codex App-server are breaking the “AI only runs on your local machine” barrier. Next: real-time preview, approval, and intervention from mobile.

Terminal experiences are approaching IDE-level quality across all three tools.

4. Security Models: From “Trust/Don’t Trust” to “Programmable Policy”

Claude Code’s hook system is the most flexible; Gemini’s SandboxManager + admin-policy takes a system-level isolation approach. Both directions may converge.

Claude Code 2.1.81: --bare Mode, Mobile Approvals, and YOLO Mode

Mar 21, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.81: —bare Mode, Mobile Approvals, and YOLO Mode

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.81: —bare Mode, Mobile Approvals, and YOLO Mode”

2.1.81 doesn’t have any big features—just two noteworthy new flags and a pile of fixes for bugs that quietly bite you in ways you can never quite pin down. Read through each one and you’ll realize this release targets the hardest-to-notice friction in the toolchain.

Two New Flags

Section titled “Two New Flags”

--bare: Scripting Mode, Zero Overhead

Section titled “--bare: Scripting Mode, Zero Overhead”

You’re calling Claude Code with -p in CI or batch scripts, but every time you have to wait for hooks, LSP, plugin sync, and skill directory scanning. All of that makes sense in interactive mode; in an automation pipeline it’s pure waste.

--bare skips all of it:

A few conditions apply: you must provide your key via ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or apiKeyHelper in --settings—OAuth and keychain auth are unavailable in this mode. Auto-memory is also completely disabled.

The use cases are clear-cut: production pipelines, cron jobs, bulk code reviews. Anywhere you don’t need a persistent session, use --bare.

--channels: Tool Approvals Forwarded to Your Phone

Section titled “--channels: Tool Approvals Forwarded to Your Phone”

This feature requires a channel server that supports the permission capability. When that’s in place, Claude’s approval prompts for tool execution no longer block the terminal—they get sent to your phone instead.

You’re in a meeting, away from your desk, and the agent hits a step that needs confirmation. It pops up on your phone; one tap and it continues. No need to walk back to your desk.

For anyone who needs to remotely supervise an agent, this beats everything else.

Bug Fixes: A Dozen Hard-to-Explain Issues

Section titled “Bug Fixes: A Dozen Hard-to-Explain Issues”

Multi-Session OAuth Re-authentication

Section titled “Multi-Session OAuth Re-authentication”

When multiple Claude Code sessions are running simultaneously and one refreshes the OAuth token, the others would be forced to re-authenticate. Now token refreshes no longer affect other sessions.

Running multiple sessions at once is a normal workflow, and this bug would constantly interrupt you in exactly that scenario.

Two Silent Failures in Voice Mode

Section titled “Two Silent Failures in Voice Mode”
  • Retry failures would swallow the error and only show “check your network connection”—now the actual error is displayed.
  • After the server silently dropped a WebSocket connection, audio wouldn’t recover—now it automatically reconnects.

Silent failures are the hardest bugs to debug. You think it’s a network issue when really the tool is lying to you.

CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS Not Working

Section titled “CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS Not Working”

Even with this environment variable set, the structured-outputs beta header was still being sent. Proxy gateways forwarding to Vertex or Bedrock would return 400 because of it.

People actually using this variable had been getting proxy errors without knowing why. Fixed now.

Hyphens in Bash Command Strings Triggering Permission Prompts

Section titled “Hyphens in Bash Command Strings Triggering Permission Prompts”

String arguments containing hyphens (-) in commands would incorrectly trigger permission prompts. A command that should have run silently would instead require manual confirmation. These false alarms erode trust in the tool. Fixed.

Plugin Directory Deleted Mid-Session Causing Blocks

Section titled “Plugin Directory Deleted Mid-Session Causing Blocks”

If the plugin directory got deleted during a session, all subsequent submissions would hang. Plugin hooks no longer block prompt submission.

Race Condition in Background Task Output

Section titled “Race Condition in Background Task Output”

When a background agent task completed between two polling intervals, the output would hang forever. Fixed.

Worktree Session Restoration

Section titled “Worktree Session Restoration”

Restoring a session that was in a worktree now automatically switches back to that worktree. Previously it wouldn’t, and you’d have to cd manually.

/btw Dropping Pasted Content

Section titled “/btw Dropping Pasted Content”

Using /btw during an active response would fail to include the pasted text. Fixed.

Clipboard Race Condition in tmux

Section titled “Clipboard Race Condition in tmux”

Quickly Cmd+Tabbing and then pasting would sometimes paste stale content. The clipboard copy in tmux hadn’t finished before it was read. Fixed.

Several Remote Control Fixes

Section titled “Several Remote Control Fixes”
  • Session titles were always generic names—now they’re derived from the first prompt.
  • /rename didn’t sync the title for Remote Control sessions—now it does.
  • /exit couldn’t reliably archive sessions—now it can.
  • Titles auto-refresh after the third message.

Other

Section titled “Other”
  • Terminal tab titles not updating—fixed.
  • Invisible hook attachments inflating the message count in transcript mode—fixed.

A Few Improvements

Section titled “A Few Improvements”

MCP tool calls collapsed into a single line. Read/search calls used to expand every time; now they’re merged into “Queried {server}”, expandable with Ctrl+O. Cuts down on visual noise quite a bit.

! bash mode is more discoverable. When you need to run an interactive command, Claude now proactively mentions this mode exists. No more digging through docs.

Ref-tracked plugins re-clone on every load. Ensures you get the latest version, not a stale cache.

Plan mode hides the “clear context” option by default. To bring it back, add "showClearContextOnPlanAccept": true.

MCP OAuth supports CIMD / SEP-991. For servers without Dynamic Client Registration, you can now use Client ID Metadata Document for OAuth.

Windows (including WSL in Windows Terminal) disables line-by-line streaming output. Due to rendering issues. WSL in Windows Terminal is also affected.

[VSCode] Windows PATH inheritance fix. The PATH inheritance for the Bash tool when using Git Bash had a regression in v2.1.78—now fixed.

The Last Two Words

Section titled “The Last Two Words”

YOLO mode.

As always.

References

Section titled “References”
  • Claude Code Changelog
  • Claude Code Documentation

Claude Code 2.1.80: --channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session

Mar 20, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.80: —channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.80: —channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session”

A Claude Code session has always been a conversation: you talk, the agent responds. MCP servers extended that — the agent could call external tools. But information only flowed one way, outward. The agent asked questions; servers answered them.

2.1.80 opens the reverse channel. --channels (research preview) lets MCP servers push messages into your running session. The tool that could only speak when spoken to just learned to raise its hand.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
Channels--channels (research preview) lets MCP servers push messages into your session
Skillseffort frontmatter for skills and slash commands overrides model effort level
Statuslinerate_limits field in statusline scripts shows Claude.ai usage (5-hour and 7-day windows)
Pluginssource: 'settings' declares plugin entries inline in settings.json
Plugin tipsCLI tool usage detection added alongside file pattern matching
ResumeFixed --resume dropping parallel tool results — no more [Tool result missing]
VoiceFixed WebSocket failures from Cloudflare bot detection on non-browser TLS fingerprints
APIFixed 400 errors with fine-grained tool streaming through API proxies, Bedrock, Vertex
RemoteFixed /remote-control appearing where it can’t function (gateway/third-party providers)
SandboxFixed /sandbox tab switching not responding to Tab or arrow keys
UXFaster @ file autocomplete in large repos; improved /effort, /permissions navigation
Performance~80MB memory savings on startup in 250k-file repos
SettingsFixed managed settings not applied at startup when remote-settings.json was cached
PluginsSimplified plugin install tips to single /plugin install command

The channel opens both ways

Section titled “The channel opens both ways”

MCP has been a one-way street. Your agent calls a tool, the server responds. That’s it. If something happens on the server side — a CI build fails, a deployment completes, a test suite finishes — the server has no way to tell the agent. You have to ask.

--channels changes this. An MCP server can now push a message into your active session without waiting to be called. Think about what that enables:

A deployment monitor MCP server watching your staging environment. Your agent is writing code. The deploy fails. The server pushes “deploy failed: missing env var DATABASE_URL on staging” directly into the session. The agent sees it, checks the config, fixes it.

A test runner MCP server that pushes results as they complete. Your agent doesn’t have to poll. It gets notified.

A team communication MCP server that pushes relevant Slack messages or PR review comments into your coding session.

This is a research preview, meaning the API surface may change. But the direction is clear: MCP is becoming a bidirectional messaging layer, not just a tool-calling protocol.

Skills learn to set their own pace

Section titled “Skills learn to set their own pace”

effort frontmatter in skills and slash commands lets the skill author override the model’s effort level when the skill is invoked.

Before this, effort was a global setting. You’d set it high for complex work, low for quick tasks, and toggle back and forth. Now the skill decides. A code formatting command runs at minimal effort because it doesn’t need deep reasoning. An architecture review skill demands maximum effort because shortcuts produce bad analysis.

This is a small YAML field with outsized impact. Skill authors can now design for the right level of reasoning rather than hoping the user has their effort setting dialed correctly.

Rate limits, visible

Section titled “Rate limits, visible”

rate_limits is a new field available to statusline scripts. It exposes Claude.ai’s 5-hour and 7-day usage windows with used_percentage and resets_at.

If you’ve ever been surprised by hitting a rate limit mid-task, this is the fix. Your statusline can now show something like “73% of 5h limit used, resets in 2h”. No more guessing.

This only applies to Claude.ai billing. API users with their own keys have different limits.

Plugins, declared inline

Section titled “Plugins, declared inline”

source: 'settings' is a new plugin marketplace source that lets you declare plugin entries directly in settings.json. No registry lookup, no install step. Write the plugin definition in your settings file, it’s loaded.

For teams that distribute internal plugins, this simplifies distribution. Push the settings.json change, everyone gets the plugin.

Combined with CLI tool usage detection for plugin tips (alongside existing file pattern matching), the plugin discovery story is getting smarter. Claude Code can now suggest plugins based on what CLI tools you’re running, not just what files exist in your project.

The resume fix that matters more than it sounds

Section titled “The resume fix that matters more than it sounds”

--resume was dropping parallel tool results. If your previous session had parallel tool calls, resuming it would show [Tool result missing] placeholders instead of the actual results.

This is worse than it sounds. Parallel tool calls are common in complex sessions — the agent reads multiple files at once, runs tests in parallel, searches across directories simultaneously. Losing those results on resume meant the agent lost context about what it had already done. It would re-read files, re-run searches, or worse, make decisions based on incomplete information.

Fixed. All tool_use/tool_result pairs now restore correctly.

Voice mode and API fixes

Section titled “Voice mode and API fixes”

Voice mode WebSocket connections were failing because Cloudflare’s bot detection was rejecting non-browser TLS fingerprints. Claude Code’s WebSocket client doesn’t look like a browser, so Cloudflare flagged it. Fixed by adjusting the TLS fingerprint handling.

Fine-grained tool streaming was returning 400 errors when used through API proxies, Bedrock, or Vertex. If you’re running Claude Code through enterprise infrastructure, this was likely hitting you. Fixed.

/remote-control was appearing in the command list for gateway and third-party provider deployments where it can’t actually function. Removed from those contexts.

Performance: 80MB lighter on large repos

Section titled “Performance: 80MB lighter on large repos”

Startup memory usage dropped by approximately 80MB on repositories with around 250,000 files. That’s a meaningful reduction. On a machine with 16GB of RAM running multiple Claude Code instances across different repos, this gives back roughly half a gigabyte.

The @ file autocomplete in large git repositories is also more responsive now. In repos with tens of thousands of files, there was a noticeable delay when typing @ to reference a file. Reduced.

UI polish

Section titled “UI polish”

Several navigation and display improvements:

/effort now shows what “auto” currently resolves to, matching the status bar indicator. Before, selecting “auto” gave you no feedback about what effort level was actually being used.

/permissions gained proper Tab and arrow key navigation within lists. Combined with the Tab/arrow fix for /sandbox, keyboard-driven navigation is now consistent across settings panels.

The background tasks panel responds to left arrow to close from the list view.

Plugin install tips simplified from a two-step flow to a single /plugin install command.

The settings fix you didn’t know you needed

Section titled “The settings fix you didn’t know you needed”

Managed settings — enabledPlugins, permissions.defaultMode, and policy-set environment variables — weren’t being applied at startup when remote-settings.json was cached from a prior session. If your organization manages Claude Code settings centrally, this meant fresh sessions could start with stale configuration.

This is the kind of bug that’s hard to diagnose because it’s intermittent. It only happens when the cached settings are different from the current ones. Fixed.

What this release signals

Section titled “What this release signals”

--channels is a research preview, but research previews in Claude Code have a track record of becoming stable features within a few releases. The fact that it shipped means the underlying architecture is ready.

The pattern across 2.1.80 is Claude Code becoming infrastructure rather than just a tool. Channels make it a message bus. Effort frontmatter makes skills self-describing. Rate limit visibility makes it observable. Inline plugin declarations make it configurable without external dependencies.

Each of these alone is a nice improvement. Together, they’re building blocks for something that looks less like a CLI and more like a development platform.

Update with claude update. If you build MCP servers, --channels is worth experimenting with now. If you write skills, add effort frontmatter. If you’ve been flying blind on rate limits, configure your statusline.
