Claude Code 2.1.74: Memory Leak Plugged, OAuth Repaired, RTL Text Fixed

Mar 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.74: Memory Leak Plugged, OAuth Repaired, RTL Text Fixed

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.74: Memory Leak Plugged, OAuth Repaired, RTL Text Fixed”

Your Claude Code process was quietly eating memory. Not because your prompts were getting longer or your context was growing — streaming API response buffers were never freed when you cancelled a generation early. On the Node.js/npm code path, RSS grew without bound. 2.1.74 fixes that, along with a set of other bugs that sound routine until one of them bites you.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
MemoryStreaming response buffers now released on early termination — no more unbounded RSS growth
MCP OAuthTwo fixes: hanging on port conflict, and silent failure after refresh token expiry
SecurityManaged policy ask rules can no longer be bypassed by user allow rules or skill allowed-tools
Agent configFull model IDs (e.g., claude-opus-4-5) now accepted in agent frontmatter and --agents JSON
Voice modemacOS native binary includes audio-input entitlement — microphone permission prompt works
RTL textHebrew, Arabic, and other RTL scripts render correctly in Windows Terminal, conhost, and VS Code
Windows LSPMalformed file URIs fixed — language servers work again
/contextNew actionable suggestions: identifies context-heavy tools, memory bloat, capacity warnings
autoMemoryNew autoMemoryDirectory setting for custom auto-memory storage location

The memory leak

Section titled “The memory leak”

This is the headliner. On the Node.js/npm code path, streaming API response buffers were not released when the generator was terminated early. If you cancelled a generation mid-stream, the buffer stayed allocated. Do that enough times in a long session, and RSS grew without bound.

The fix is straightforward: buffers are now properly released when the generator is terminated. If you’ve been noticing your Claude Code process gradually consuming more memory over multi-hour sessions, this was likely the cause.

This is distinct from the native bash parser memory leak fixed in 2.1.72. That one accumulated during command parsing. This one accumulated during response streaming. Both contributed to the same symptom — a process that got heavier over time.

MCP OAuth: two separate problems

Section titled “MCP OAuth: two separate problems”

MCP OAuth authentication had two bugs, each capable of silently breaking your integrations.

Port conflict hang. When the OAuth callback port was already in use, authentication would hang indefinitely. No error, no timeout, just a process waiting for a callback that would never arrive. The fix detects the conflict and fails with a clear message.

Token refresh failure. Some OAuth servers (Slack is the notable example) return errors with HTTP 200 status codes. The refresh logic treated any 200 response as success, so when a refresh token expired, it would silently fail to re-authenticate. The fix now inspects the response body, detects the error, and prompts for re-authentication.

If you’ve had MCP integrations that worked for weeks and then quietly stopped, this is probably why.

Managed policy bypass

Section titled “Managed policy bypass”

A security fix. Managed policy ask rules — the ones set by administrators — could be bypassed by user-level allow rules or by skill allowed-tools declarations. The hierarchy is now enforced: managed policies take precedence regardless of what users or skills declare.

This matters for enterprise deployments where administrators set policy boundaries they expect to be respected.

Agent model configuration

Section titled “Agent model configuration”

Full model IDs like claude-opus-4-5 were silently ignored in agent frontmatter model: fields and --agents JSON configuration. The agent would fall back to its default model without warning. Agents now accept the same model values as the --model flag.

If you’ve configured agents with specific model IDs and wondered why they weren’t using the right model, this was the bug.

Voice mode on macOS

Section titled “Voice mode on macOS”

The macOS native binary was missing the audio-input entitlement. For users whose terminal had never been granted microphone permission, voice mode silently failed — no error, no permission prompt, just nothing happening when you tried to speak.

The binary now includes the entitlement, so macOS prompts for microphone access as expected.

SessionEnd hooks timeout

Section titled “SessionEnd hooks timeout”

SessionEnd hooks were killed after 1.5 seconds on exit regardless of the hook.timeout setting. If your cleanup hook needed more than 1.5 seconds, it got killed silently. The timeout is now configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_SESSIONEND_HOOKS_TIMEOUT_MS.

RTL text rendering

Section titled “RTL text rendering”

Hebrew, Arabic, and other right-to-left scripts were not rendering correctly in Windows Terminal, conhost, and VS Code’s integrated terminal. This is a fix that makes Claude Code usable for a set of users who were previously dealing with garbled output.

Windows LSP

Section titled “Windows LSP”

Language server protocol servers were not working on Windows due to malformed file URIs. If you use LSP features in Claude Code on Windows, this was why they were broken.

Plugin ecosystem

Section titled “Plugin ecosystem”

Three plugin fixes:

  • /plugin install was failing inside the REPL for marketplace plugins with local sources
  • Marketplace update was not syncing git submodules, breaking plugins that use submodule dependencies
  • --plugin-dir local dev copies now override installed marketplace plugins with the same name (unless force-enabled by managed settings)

The override change is a workflow improvement for plugin developers: your local copy takes precedence during development.

Unknown slash commands

Section titled “Unknown slash commands”

Previously, typing an unknown slash command with arguments would silently drop your input. The text you typed after the command just disappeared. Now it shows your input as a warning, so at least you know what happened.

New: actionable /context suggestions

Section titled “New: actionable /context suggestions”

The /context command now identifies context-heavy tools, memory bloat, and capacity warnings, and provides specific optimization tips. Instead of just showing you how much context you’re using, it tells you what to do about it.

New: autoMemoryDirectory setting

Section titled “New: autoMemoryDirectory setting”

You can now configure a custom directory for auto-memory storage with the autoMemoryDirectory setting. Useful if you want auto-memory stored somewhere other than the default location.

VS Code improvements

Section titled “VS Code improvements”
  • Delete button now works for Untitled sessions
  • Scroll wheel responsiveness improved in the integrated terminal with terminal-aware acceleration

What 2.1.74 signals

Section titled “What 2.1.74 signals”

Where 2.1.72 was a broad sweep across 60+ items, 2.1.74 is targeted. The fixes cluster around trust-critical systems: memory management, authentication, security policy enforcement, and cross-platform compatibility.

The common thread is silence. The memory leak didn’t announce itself. OAuth failures returned 200 OK. Policy bypasses worked without errors. Voice mode failed without a prompt. The bugs in this release are the kind that erode confidence gradually — you don’t know what’s wrong, you just know something feels off.

Fixing these specifically, and fixing them quickly after 2.1.72, suggests a team that understands which bugs matter most. Not the ones that crash loudly, but the ones that fail quietly.

Claude Code 2.1.72: 60+ Fixes, an Effort Rethink, and a 12x Cache Win

Mar 10, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.72: 60+ Fixes, an Effort Rethink, and a 12x Cache Win

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.72: 60+ Fixes, an Effort Rethink, and a 12x Cache Win”

Sixty-plus items in a single changelog. No new model. No paradigm shift. Just a team that looked at their bug tracker, their performance dashboards, and their user feedback queue, and decided to clear the table.

The numbers first

Section titled “The numbers first”

Before diving into categories, here’s what stands out at a glance:

MetricDetail
Bug fixes60+ across sandbox, hooks, plugins, voice, sessions
Bundle sizeReduced by ~510 KB
Prompt cache costUp to 12x reduction in SDK query() calls
Bash parsingSwitched to native module — faster init, zero memory leak
Effort levelsSimplified from 4 to 3 (removed “max”)
Parallel tool resilienceFailed Read/WebFetch/Glob no longer kills siblings

This is the largest patch release Claude Code has shipped. The scope tells you something about the surface area the tool now covers.

Effort gets a redesign

Section titled “Effort gets a redesign”

The effort system went from four levels to three: low, medium, high. The “max” level is gone. New symbols replace the old ones: a hollow circle for low, a half-filled circle for medium, a filled circle for high. The persistent icon in the status bar was replaced by a brief notification that fades.

Removing “max” is a design call worth noting. Four levels created a false precision problem. Users agonized over the difference between “high” and “max” when there wasn’t a meaningful one in practice. Three levels map cleanly to how people actually think about task complexity.

The 12x prompt cache fix

Section titled “The 12x prompt cache fix”

A bug in SDK query() calls was invalidating the prompt cache far more often than necessary. The fix reduces input token costs by up to 12x for applications built on the Claude Code SDK. If you’ve been running Claude Code through the SDK and noticed higher-than-expected bills, this is why.

This is the kind of fix that doesn’t make demos look better but makes CFOs happier.

Native bash parser

Section titled “Native bash parser”

The bash command parser was rewritten as a native module. Two concrete improvements: faster initialization (no JS-based parser warm-up) and elimination of a memory leak that accumulated over long sessions.

If you run Claude Code for hours at a stretch, you’ve probably noticed the process slowly consuming more memory. This was a contributor.

Sandbox and permission hardening

Section titled “Sandbox and permission hardening”

The permission system got serious attention. Multiple fixes address cases where the security boundary wasn’t matching user expectations:

  • Wildcard permission rules now correctly match commands containing heredocs, embedded newlines, or no arguments
  • sandbox.excludedCommands works with env var prefixes
  • “Always allow” no longer suggests overly broad prefixes for nested CLI tools
  • Deny rules apply to all command forms consistently
  • File write operations that should have prompted now do
  • Output redirections to allowlisted directories (like /tmp/claude/) no longer prompt unnecessarily

The pattern here is telling. These aren’t theoretical vulnerabilities. They’re gaps discovered by users who actually configure custom sandbox rules, use heredocs in bash, and run nested CLI tools. The fixes tighten the model without adding friction for standard usage.

Hooks get reliable

Section titled “Hooks get reliable”

Hooks had a rough patch. This release fixes six separate issues:

  1. transcript_path pointed to the wrong directory for resumed or forked sessions
  2. Agent prompt was silently deleted from settings.json on every settings write
  3. PostToolUse block reasons displayed twice
  4. Async hooks didn’t receive stdin with bash read -r
  5. Validation error messages showed examples that themselves failed validation
  6. Skill hooks fired twice per event when a hooks-enabled skill was invoked by the model

If you’ve built automation around hooks, item 2 was especially painful. Your agent prompt would vanish after any settings change, with no error and no warning.

Plugin fixes across platforms

Section titled “Plugin fixes across platforms”

The plugin system saw five fixes, several targeting Windows:

  • Installation no longer fails with EEXIST on Windows OneDrive folders
  • Marketplace no longer blocks user-scope installs when a project-scope install exists
  • CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR no longer creates literal ~ directories
  • plugin.json with marketplace-only fields no longer fails to load
  • Marketplace git URLs without .git suffix now work (Azure DevOps, AWS CodeCommit)

The OneDrive fix is a good example of a bug you’d never find in a test lab. OneDrive syncs create file system conditions that normal installations don’t encounter. You only find this when real Windows users install plugins in their actual home directories.

Parallel tool calls stop cascading

Section titled “Parallel tool calls stop cascading”

Previously, if a Read, WebFetch, or Glob tool failed during parallel execution, it would cancel all its sibling tool calls. Now only Bash errors cascade. The other tools fail independently.

This is architecturally significant. Parallel tool calls are how Claude Code stays fast — running multiple file reads or web fetches simultaneously. Letting one failure kill the batch was pessimistic and wasteful. The new behavior: if one file doesn’t exist, the other reads still complete.

Voice mode cleanup

Section titled “Voice mode cleanup”

Five separate voice fixes:

  • Occasional input lag eliminated
  • False “No speech detected” errors after releasing push-to-talk resolved
  • Stale transcripts no longer re-fill the prompt after submission
  • Transcription accuracy improved for repo names and common dev terms (regex, OAuth, JSON)
  • Voice input transcription accuracy improvements for technical vocabulary

The transcription accuracy fix is worth calling out. Saying “regex” or “OAuth” and having it transcribed correctly matters for a tool that needs to act on what you say.

Session and UI fixes

Section titled “Session and UI fixes”

The long tail of session management fixes:

  • --continue now resumes from the most recent point after --compact
  • Backgrounded Ctrl+B queries no longer lose their transcript or corrupt the new conversation after /clear
  • /clear only kills foreground tasks now, leaving background agents running
  • /model displays results even while Claude is working
  • Digit keys type in plan mode permission prompts instead of selecting menu options
  • Escape key no longer becomes unresponsive after cancelling a query
  • Double Ctrl+C exits even with background agents running
  • Session titles handle multi-line first messages correctly
  • Queued messages show attached images properly

Config and workflow improvements

Section titled “Config and workflow improvements”

Several quality-of-life changes:

  • /config now uses Escape to cancel, Enter to save and close, Space to toggle settings
  • Up-arrow history shows current session’s messages first in concurrent sessions
  • /plan accepts an optional description argument (/plan fix the auth bug) that enters plan mode and starts immediately
  • w key in /copy writes focused selection directly to a file, bypassing clipboard (useful over SSH)
  • CLAUDE.md HTML comments (<!-- ... -->) are now hidden from Claude when auto-injected, but remain visible when read with the Read tool
  • CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CRON environment variable stops scheduled cron jobs mid-session

The /plan shorthand and the /copy file write are small changes that compress common workflows. The CLAUDE.md comment behavior is more subtle — you can now leave notes for humans in your CLAUDE.md that Claude won’t see during normal operation, but can still access if explicitly asked to read the file.

Additional fixes

Section titled “Additional fixes”
  • Team agents inherit the leader’s model
  • “Always Allow” no longer saves permission rules that never match again
  • Feedback survey appears less frequently in long sessions
  • --effort CLI flag no longer gets reset by unrelated settings writes on startup
  • Worktree isolation fixed: Task tool resume restores cwd, background task notifications include worktreePath and worktreeBranch
  • Session crashes fixed for files containing U+2028/U+2029 characters
  • Terminal title no longer cleared on exit when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE was set
  • Oversized and truncated images from Bash data-URL output fixed
  • Crash on resuming sessions with Bedrock API errors fixed
  • Intermittent validation errors on Edit, Bash, and Grep tool inputs fixed
  • Marketplace clone failures now show diagnostic info even without git stderr

VS Code improvements

Section titled “VS Code improvements”
  • Scroll speed in integrated terminals now matches native terminals
  • Shift+Enter inserts a newline instead of submitting for users with older keybindings
  • Effort level indicator added to the input border
  • vscode://anthropic.claude-code/open URI handler opens a new Claude Code tab programmatically, with optional prompt and session query parameters

The URI handler is interesting for toolchain integration. You can now deep-link into Claude Code from other tools, scripts, or documentation.

CPU and memory

Section titled “CPU and memory”

Two infrastructure improvements: better CPU utilization in long sessions, and the memory leak fix from the native bash parser. Together they mean Claude Code degrades less over multi-hour sessions.

What 60+ fixes in one release means

Section titled “What 60+ fixes in one release means”

A changelog this large isn’t about any single item. It’s about what the aggregate signals.

The bugs span six distinct subsystems: sandbox permissions, hooks, plugins, voice, sessions, and VS Code integration. The fixes reference Windows, SSH, OneDrive, Azure DevOps, Bedrock, and multiple OAuth providers. The edge cases involve heredocs, U+2028 characters, literal tilde directories, and mingw-style paths from two releases ago that still needed cleanup.

This is what a tool looks like when it’s being used in environments its authors didn’t originally anticipate. And the response — fixing all of it in one release instead of triaging it across quarters — suggests a team that treats reliability as a feature, not a tax.

The prompt cache fix alone will save some teams meaningful money. The sandbox hardening makes the tool safer for enterprise use. The hooks fixes make automation reliable enough to depend on. None of these are exciting on their own. Together, they’re the difference between a tool you try and a tool you commit to.

Claude Code 2.1.71: /loop Turns Your Terminal Into a Self-Driving Agent

Mar 7, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.71: /loop Turns Your Terminal Into a Self-Driving Agent

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.71: /loop Turns Your Terminal Into a Self-Driving Agent”

Claude Code just learned to set its own alarm clock.

Version 2.1.71 shipped /loop, a command that schedules recurring prompts inside your session. Type /loop 5m check the deploy and walk away. Claude checks every five minutes, reports back when something changes. That single addition changes what Claude Code is.

The headline: /loop and cron scheduling

Section titled “The headline: /loop and cron scheduling”

The /loop command is a bundled skill that converts a natural-language interval into a cron expression and runs it in the background.

Supported intervals: s (seconds, rounded to nearest minute), m (minutes), h (hours), d (days). If you skip the interval, it defaults to every 10 minutes.

You can also loop over other commands:

Every 20 minutes, Claude runs your PR review skill automatically.

For one-shot reminders, just ask in natural language:

Under the hood, three new tools power this:

ToolPurpose
CronCreateSchedule a task with a 5-field cron expression
CronListList all active scheduled tasks
CronDeleteCancel a task by its 8-character ID

A session can hold up to 50 scheduled tasks. They fire between your turns, not mid-response. All times use your local timezone. Tasks auto-expire after 3 days.

One design decision worth noting: scheduled tasks are session-scoped. Close the terminal, everything is gone. This is intentional. For persistent scheduling, Anthropic points you to Desktop scheduled tasks or GitHub Actions. The session scope keeps the blast radius small.

Voice mode gets a rebindable key

Section titled “Voice mode gets a rebindable key”

The voice:pushToTalk keybinding is now configurable in keybindings.json. Default is still space, but you can set it to modifier+letter combos like meta+k that have zero interference with normal typing.

This matters if you use voice mode during coding sessions. Previously, the space bar doing double duty was a constant friction point.

Bash allowlist expansion

Section titled “Bash allowlist expansion”

These commands are now auto-approved without permission prompts:

fmt, comm, cmp, numfmt, expr, test, printf, getconf, seq, tsort, pr

Most are POSIX text-processing utilities. Adding them means Claude can do more string manipulation, number formatting, and comparison operations without interrupting your flow.

Bug fixes that reveal scale

Section titled “Bug fixes that reveal scale”

The bug list in 2.1.71 is long. These are not edge cases from a demo — they come from a large user base hitting real conditions.

Session stability:

  • Fixed stdin freeze in long-running sessions where keystrokes stop being processed but the process stays alive. If you’ve ever had Claude Code go deaf after an hour, this is the fix
  • Fixed a 5-8 second startup freeze for users with voice mode enabled, caused by CoreAudio initialization blocking the main thread after system wake
  • Fixed startup UI freeze when many claude.ai proxy connectors refresh an expired OAuth token simultaneously

Multi-instance and forking:

  • Fixed forked conversations (/fork) sharing the same plan file, which caused plan edits in one fork to overwrite the other. If you use /fork to explore parallel approaches, this was silently corrupting your work
  • Fixed plugin installations being lost when running multiple Claude Code instances
  • Fixed claude.ai connectors failing to reconnect after OAuth token refresh

Permission and parsing edge cases:

  • Fixed false-positive permission prompts for compound bash commands containing heredoc commit messages
  • Fixed /plugin marketplace add owner/repo@ref incorrectly parsing @ — previously only # worked as a ref separator
  • Fixed duplicate entries in /permissions Workspace tab when the same directory is added with and without a trailing slash

Print mode and agents:

  • Fixed --print hanging forever when team agents are configured — the exit loop no longer waits on long-lived in_process_teammate tasks
  • Fixed background agent completion notifications missing the output file path, making it hard for parent agents to recover results after context compaction

UI cleanup:

  • Fixed “Tool loaded.” appearing in the REPL after every ToolSearch call
  • Fixed duplicate output in Bash tool error messages when commands exit with non-zero status
  • Fixed Chrome extension auto-detection getting permanently stuck on “not installed” after running on a machine without local Chrome
  • Fixed prompting for cd <cwd> && git ... on Windows when the model uses a mingw-style path

Performance improvements

Section titled “Performance improvements”
ChangeImpact
Native image processor loadingDeferred to first use, faster startup
Bridge session reconnectionCompletes in seconds after laptop wake, was up to 10 minutes
Plugin uninstall scopeNow writes to .claude/settings.local.json, doesn’t affect teammates
MCP server deduplicationSkips duplicate plugin servers, prevents double connections
Debug logging/debug toggles mid-session, no longer written by default
Startup notificationsSuppressed for unauthenticated org-registered connectors

What this release actually means

Section titled “What this release actually means”

Two patterns are visible across the last few Claude Code releases.

First, the tool is moving from reactive to proactive. Previous versions added background agents. Now you get scheduled tasks. The trajectory is clear: Claude Code wants to be a runtime, not just a REPL.

Second, the bug fixes are getting more specific. stdin freezes in long sessions. OAuth token race conditions across multiple proxy connectors. Plan file conflicts in forked conversations. These are bugs that exist only at scale, only with power users, only in production conditions. They signal that the user base has grown past the early-adopter stage.

The combination of /loop and the reliability fixes means you can now trust Claude Code to run unsupervised for longer periods. That’s a meaningful change in how you work with it.

Claude Code 2.1.70: The Most Boring Changelog Is the Most Bullish Signal

Mar 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.70: The Most Boring Changelog Is the Most Bullish Signal

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.70: The Most Boring Changelog Is the Most Bullish Signal”

Claude Code 2.1.70 shipped with zero new headline features. Over 20 bug fixes, a handful of performance improvements, and some VS Code polish. On paper, the least exciting release in months. In practice, maybe the most important one.

What everyone assumed

Section titled “What everyone assumed”

The AI coding tool space has a pattern. New release drops, Twitter lights up, everyone debates whether the demo is real or cherry-picked. We’ve been trained to expect fireworks from every changelog. A new model, a bigger context window, a feature that “changes everything.”

2.1.70 breaks that pattern.

What the changelog actually says

Section titled “What the changelog actually says”

The changelog reads like a bug tracker, not a press release.

API and proxy compatibility:

  • Fixed API 400 errors when using ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with third-party gateways — tool search now correctly detects proxy endpoints and disables tool_reference blocks
  • Fixed the effort parameter crashing on custom Bedrock inference profiles or model identifiers that don’t match standard Claude naming patterns
  • Fixed empty model responses right after ToolSearch — the server was rendering tool schemas with system-prompt-style tags at the prompt tail, confusing models into stopping early
  • Fixed prompt-cache bust when an MCP server with instructions connects after the first turn

Cross-platform fixes:

  • Fixed clipboard corrupting non-ASCII text (CJK, emoji) on Windows/WSL by switching to PowerShell’s Set-Clipboard
  • Fixed Enter inserting a newline instead of submitting when typing over a slow SSH connection
  • Fixed extra VS Code windows opening at startup on Windows from the integrated terminal
  • Fixed voice mode failing on Windows native binary with “native audio module could not be loaded”
  • Fixed push-to-talk not activating on session start when voiceEnabled: true was set

UI and developer ergonomics:

  • Fixed markdown links containing #NNN references pointing to the current repository instead of the linked URL
  • Fixed repeated “Model updated to Opus 4.6” notification when a legacy model string was pinned in .claude/settings.json
  • Fixed plugins showing as inaccurately installed in /plugin
  • Fixed plugins showing “not found in marketplace” errors on fresh startup by auto-refreshing after marketplace installation
  • Fixed /security-review failing with unknown option merge-base on older git versions
  • Fixed /color command having no way to reset — /color default, /color gray, /color reset, and /color none now restore defaults
  • Fixed a performance regression in the AskUserQuestion preview dialog that re-ran markdown rendering on every keystroke
  • Fixed feature flags read during early startup never refreshing their disk cache, causing stale values across sessions
  • Fixed permissions defaultMode values other than acceptEdits or plan being applied in Claude Code Remote — they’re now ignored
  • Fixed skill listing re-injected on every --resume (~600 tokens saved per resume)
  • Fixed teleport marker not rendering in VS Code teleported sessions

These are not demo bugs. These are the bugs you find when thousands of developers use the tool daily, on different operating systems, over unreliable connections, plugged into third-party infrastructure.

The performance story

Section titled “The performance story”

The numbers tell the same story as the bug fixes.

ImprovementImpact
Prompt input re-rendersReduced by ~74%
Startup memory (no custom CA certs)Reduced by ~426KB
Remote Control polling (while connected)From 1-2s to 10min (~300x reduction)
Skill listing on --resume~600 tokens saved per resume
CompactionNow preserves images, enabling prompt cache reuse
Microphone error messagesNow distinguishes silence from “no speech detected”
/renameWorks while Claude is processing instead of being queued

None of this is visible to someone watching a demo. All of it is visible to someone using the tool eight hours a day.

VS Code goes deeper

Section titled “VS Code goes deeper”

Three additions that signal where the team sees the primary surface heading.

Session management — A spark icon in the VS Code activity bar lists all Claude Code sessions. Sessions open as full editors, not just terminal panes.

Plan views — Plans get a full markdown document view with comment support. You can add feedback directly on plans instead of switching to the chat panel.

Native MCP management — Use /mcp in the chat panel to enable/disable servers, reconnect, and manage OAuth authentication. No more switching to terminal for MCP configuration.

These aren’t bolt-on features. They’re investments in making Claude Code feel native to VS Code rather than grafted on.

The quiet flex at the end

Section titled “The quiet flex at the end”

The last line of the changelog is two words: YOLO mode.

After 30+ fixes for edge cases that most teams would have shipped around for months, it lands differently. Not as a gimmick, but as a team that earned the right to have some fun after grinding through the backlog.

What this means for developers evaluating AI coding tools

Section titled “What this means for developers evaluating AI coding tools”

Next time you see an AI tool changelog full of bug fixes instead of flashy features, read it more carefully. A polish-heavy release is the strongest vote of confidence a team can make — it means the core works and they’re betting on long-term adoption over short-term hype.

The bugs they fixed tell you more about the tool’s maturity than any feature announcement ever could.

Claude Code 2.1.70 is the kind of release you don’t tweet about. It’s the kind you update to.

The Secret Inside 176 Updates: Claude Code's Changelog Is an Agent OS Blueprint

Mar 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Secret Inside 176 Updates: Claude Code’s Changelog Is an Agent OS Blueprint

Section titled “The Secret Inside 176 Updates: Claude Code’s Changelog Is an Agent OS Blueprint”

In 2025, Claude Code shipped 176 updates. From February’s public beta to December’s v2.0 — one update every two days, on average.

You probably didn’t read a single one carefully. Neither did I.

A developer named Oikon did. He read all 176 updates start to finish and wrote a summary. His conclusion: context engineering is the thread running through everything.

He got half of it right. The other half he didn’t unpack — these 176 updates aren’t a feature list. They’re a construction blueprint. What Anthropic is building is much bigger than a “coding assistant.”

A Different Lens for Reading Changelogs

Section titled “A Different Lens for Reading Changelogs”

A recent thread by @yan5xu laid out a framework for dissecting any job. The core claim: all work follows the same loop.

Research → Decision → Planning → Execution → Feedback → Review

Whether you’re in operations, development, content creation, or finance — break your work into these six steps and everything fits. The key question at each step: are you making a judgment call, or are you just moving data from A to B?

He also introduced a three-layer model:

  • Manager (LLM): understands intent, makes plans
  • Charter (code and scripts): write once, execute forever
  • Employee (tools and APIs): follows instructions, doesn’t think

Connect all three layers, and the Agent runs the entire loop end-to-end. Leave them disconnected, and the LLM — no matter how smart — is a manager locked in a windowless room. It can’t see outside. It can’t change anything.

Apply this framework to Claude Code’s changelog, and something clicks.

Every Milestone Fills a Cell in the Table

Section titled “Every Milestone Fills a Cell in the Table”

I mapped Claude Code’s major features against the six-step loop. It’s not a perfect one-to-one, but the direction is clear:

Work StepClaude Code CapabilityKey Version/Feature
ResearchMCP connecting 300+ external services; Web Search; filesystem accessMCP protocol launched 2024.11, integrations grew from 100K to 8M
DecisionPlan Mode (think before acting); CLAUDE.md rule memoryPlan Mode mid-2025, Opus Plan Mode later enhanced
PlanningSkills templates; /context command for project context loadingSkills (SKILL.md) 2026.01, /context late 2025
ExecutionBash tools, file editing, Subagents for parallel executionSubagents late 2025, Background agents 2025.12
FeedbackHooks as quality gates; Sandbox for secure executionHooks system 2025, Sandbox early 2026
ReviewCLAUDE.md persistent memory; auto memory; session historyCLAUDE.md since v0.2, auto memory iteratively improved

Every step has tooling. Every tool can be called programmatically. The LLM sits in the middle, stringing the entire chain together.

This isn’t “helping you with a step.” This is the entire task running autonomously.

What the Three Layers Look Like in Claude Code

Section titled “What the Three Layers Look Like in Claude Code”

Back to the manager, charter, employee model:

Manager layer = Claude (the LLM itself)

Claude understands your intent. You say “migrate this API from REST to GraphQL,” and it breaks the work into steps, picks tools, sequences execution. Plan Mode makes it think before acting — no more charging in blind.

Charter layer = CLAUDE.md + Skills + Hooks

CLAUDE.md is project memory — coding standards, architecture conventions, common commands. Written once, auto-loaded every session. Skills are reusable workflow templates — test procedures, code review processes, deployment flows, packaged up, triggered by a single command. Hooks are quality gates — auto-run lint before commits, check security before command execution. Pure deterministic logic, no LLM involved.

Employee layer = MCP + Bash + Subagents + Plugins

MCP connects Claude to everything you use — databases, Jira, GitHub, Sentry, Slack, 300+ integrations. Bash tools let it run commands directly in the terminal. Subagents are isolated Claude instances, each handling a subtask without interfering with each other. Plugins bundle all of this into distributable units — install one plugin, get LSP, MCP, Skills, and Hooks all at once.

All three layers are in place. Each went through multiple iteration cycles in 2025.

How the Creator Uses It

Section titled “How the Creator Uses It”

Boris Cherny created Claude Code. He’s the Head of Claude Code at Anthropic. Before that, five years as Principal Engineer at Meta. Author of Programming TypeScript.

His daily workflow: 15 to 20 parallel Opus sessions running simultaneously. Five in local terminal windows, another 5 to 10 on Anthropic’s website. Each session runs on its own git worktree, fully isolated. He calls this “the single biggest productivity unlock.”

That’s not “using a tool.” That’s managing a team.

He also mentioned two directions the Claude Code team is actively pushing: long-running tasks and swarm capabilities. Both at the demo stage.

Long-running tasks mean the Agent doesn’t need you watching. Start a migration, close the terminal, go to your meeting. When you come back, the job is done, results waiting for review.

Swarm means multiple Agents working together. Not one Agent doing tasks sequentially — multiple Agents processing different parts of a large task in parallel.

What Happened in Early 2026

Section titled “What Happened in Early 2026”

The pace didn’t slow down:

  • Sandbox mode shipped — Bash tools now run in a security sandbox on Linux and Mac
  • HTTP Hooks — Hooks can POST JSON to remote URLs and receive JSON back, no longer limited to local shell commands
  • Enterprise MCP controls — IT teams can set MCP allowlists and denylists
  • Voice input supports 20 languages
  • Plugin search and SHA pinning — the plugin ecosystem is formalizing
  • Sonnet 4.6 launched — better agentic search, fewer tokens, 1M context window
  • Opus 4 and 4.1 retired — users auto-migrated to Opus 4.6

Every update reinforces the three layers: smarter manager (Sonnet 4.6), more complete charter (HTTP Hooks), safer employees (Sandbox).

Your Turn to Fill the Table

Section titled “Your Turn to Fill the Table”

Back to @yan5xu’s methodology. He nailed it: designing an Agent is essentially filling out a table.

Research: Where does your data come from? Is there an API? Can you pull it automatically?

Decision: What are your classification rules? How do you handle edge cases?

Planning: What’s the output format? Where does it go?

Execution: Which API to call? Which page to interact with?

Feedback: How do you confirm it worked? How do you get alerted on failures?

Review: How does this run’s deviation become next run’s automatic rule?

Claude Code’s changelog tells you this: every cell in that table now has a tool to fill it. MCP fills research and execution. Plan Mode fills decision and planning. Hooks fill feedback. CLAUDE.md fills review.

You only need to do one thing: break your own work into these six steps and find where you’re still acting as the pipeline.

Start with the step that annoys you most. Not necessarily the most time-consuming one — but the one that blocks your morning, the one that makes you procrastinate before you even begin.

Hand that step to an Agent. Wait for the morning when you open your laptop and that task is already done. Not “efficiency improved.” The task is gone.

Once you feel that, the rest follows naturally.

Claude Code 2.1.69: Twenty Small Cuts That Sharpen the Platform

Mar 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.69: Twenty Small Cuts That Sharpen the Platform

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.69: Twenty Small Cuts That Sharpen the Platform”

Twenty features. None of them headline-worthy on its own. That’s exactly why this release matters.

Between February 5 and February 28, Claude Code shipped a multi-agent platform — Opus 4.6, agent teams, worktree isolation, remote control, persistent memory, HTTP hooks. Eight releases in fifteen days. Impressive, and rough around the edges.

2.1.69 (March 4) does the harder work: it makes that platform comfortable. Skills know where they live. Hooks know which agent triggered them. Your terminal shows what effort level is active. Plugins reload without restarting. These are ergonomics — and ergonomics decide whether powerful tools get used or shelved.

Skills Ecosystem

Section titled “Skills Ecosystem”

Two additions that change how skills work in practice.

/claude-api skill — A built-in skill for building applications with the Claude API and Anthropic SDK. Instead of remembering SDK patterns or searching docs, you get guided assistance for API integration directly inside Claude Code.

${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} variable — Skills can now reference their own directory in SKILL.md content. Before this, a skill that needed to load a template or data file from its own directory had to use absolute paths or fragile relative references. Now:

This matters for portable, shareable skills. A skill published as a plugin works the same regardless of where it’s installed.

Plugin Infrastructure

Section titled “Plugin Infrastructure”

Four changes that make the plugin ecosystem more enterprise-ready.

/reload-plugins — Activate pending plugin changes without restarting Claude Code. During plugin development, this cuts the feedback loop from “restart session, lose context” to “reload, keep working.”

pluginTrustMessage — Managed settings can now append organization-specific context to the plugin trust warning shown before installation. An enterprise admin can add “Only install plugins from our internal marketplace at plugins.corp.internal” directly into the trust dialog.

pathPattern in strictKnownMarketplaces — Regex matching for file and directory marketplace sources, alongside existing hostPattern restrictions. More granular control over where plugins come from.

git-subdir plugin source — Point to a subdirectory within a git repo. A monorepo with five plugins no longer needs five separate repos.

Hooks Evolution

Section titled “Hooks Evolution”

Three features that give hooks better awareness of the platform’s internal state.

InstructionsLoaded hook event — Fires when CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules/*.md files are loaded into context. An enterprise security team can audit which instruction files are active. A development workflow can trigger actions when project rules change.

agent_id and agent_type in hook events — Every hook event now carries the identity of the agent that triggered it. agent_id for subagents, agent_type for both subagents and --agent sessions. A PreToolUse hook can now apply different policies to different agents — let the code-writer use Bash freely, restrict the code-reviewer to Read-only.

worktree field in status line hook commands — When running in a --worktree session, hooks receive name, path, branch, and original repo directory. A CI integration can track which worktree is running what.

UX Polish

Section titled “UX Polish”

Small changes to the daily interaction surface.

Ctrl+U on empty bash prompt exits bash mode — Matches the existing Escape and Backspace behavior. One more muscle memory path that works as expected.

Numeric keypad support — Interview questions (those numbered option lists Claude presents) now accept input from the numeric keypad, not just the number row above QWERTY. If you’ve been jabbing the numpad and wondering why nothing happened, that’s fixed.

Effort level in spinner — The logo and spinner now display the active effort setting (e.g., “with low effort”). Before, you had to check /config to remember what effort level was active. Now it’s visible whenever Claude is thinking.

Agent name in terminal title — When using claude --agent, the terminal title shows the agent name. With multiple terminal tabs running different agents, you can tell them apart at a glance.

Claude Code Desktop prompt — A one-time startup suggestion for Claude Code Desktop on macOS and Windows. Shown up to 3 times, then dismissed permanently. Low friction, easy to ignore.

Configuration

Section titled “Configuration”

Two settings for specific environments.

sandbox.enableWeakerNetworkIsolation (macOS only) — Allows Go programs like gh, gcloud, and terraform to verify TLS certificates when using a custom MITM proxy with httpProxyPort. Corporate networks with TLS inspection proxies need this.

includeGitInstructions — Removes built-in commit and PR workflow instructions from Claude’s system prompt. Also available as CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_GIT_INSTRUCTIONS env var. Useful if you have custom commit workflows in your CLAUDE.md and don’t want Claude’s defaults conflicting.

Remote Control Enhancement

Section titled “Remote Control Enhancement”

Optional name argument — /remote-control My Project or --name "My Project" sets a custom session title visible in claude.ai/code. When you’re monitoring multiple remote sessions from your phone, names beat auto-generated IDs.

The Pattern

Section titled “The Pattern”

Read the features individually and you see a maintenance release. Read them together and you see something deliberate: every change targets the interaction surface between you and the platform.

LayerWhat shippedWhy it matters
Skills/claude-api, ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}Skills become portable and self-aware
Plugins/reload-plugins, trust customization, git-subdirPlugin development and enterprise deployment get practical
HooksInstructionsLoaded, agent identity, worktree contextHooks can make agent-aware, context-aware decisions
UXCtrl+U, numpad, effort display, agent name in titleDaily friction removed from the interaction surface
ConfigTLS proxy support, git instruction toggleEdge-case environments work without workarounds

The multi-agent platform from 2.1.32–2.1.63 was powerful. 2.1.69 makes it fit your hands.

What to Try

Section titled “What to Try”
  1. /reload-plugins — If you develop or test plugins, this saves you restarts
  2. Effort level display — Adjust effort with /effort and watch the spinner reflect it
  3. ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} — Refactor a skill to reference its own directory for templates or data files
  4. InstructionsLoaded hook — Build a hook that logs when project instructions change
  5. Remote control naming — Name your next remote session: /remote-control "Feature Auth"

Reference

  • Hooks documentation
  • Plugins documentation
  • Remote Control

Your AI Agent Skills Are Broken. Here's the Fix.

Mar 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Your AI Agent Skills Are Broken. Here’s the Fix.

Section titled “Your AI Agent Skills Are Broken. Here’s the Fix.”

You’ve been writing skills wrong.

Not a little wrong. Fundamentally wrong. Most developers approach AI agent skills like documentation for a junior developer — dump some context, add headers, throw in examples, hope it works. The result: bloated context windows, misfiring triggers, inconsistent output.

Minko Gechev’s skills-best-practices repo treats this problem with the rigor it deserves. The core insight is simple and sharp: skills aren’t documentation. They’re programs. The runtime is an LLM.

The anatomy of a skill

Section titled “The anatomy of a skill”

Every skill follows one structure:

No README. No changelog. No library code. If a file doesn’t serve the agent at runtime, it’s waste.

SKILL.md is the brain — high-level procedures and navigation. References hold API docs and cheatsheets. Scripts handle fragile, repetitive operations where variation is a bug. Assets store templates the agent copies. That’s the entire surface area.

Discovery is where skills die

Section titled “Discovery is where skills die”

The agent sees exactly two things before deciding to load your skill: name and description. That’s 1,024 characters to determine whether your skill exists or doesn’t.

Bad description: “React skills.”

Good description: “Creates and builds React components using Tailwind CSS. Use when the user wants to update component styles or UI logic. Don’t use it for Vue, Svelte, or vanilla CSS projects.”

Notice the negative triggers. You have to tell the agent when NOT to fire. Without them, your Angular migration skill will activate on React projects. Your Python testing skill will trigger on Go code.

The name field has strict rules too: 1-64 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens only, no consecutive hyphens, and it must match the parent directory name. angular-testing lives in angular-testing/SKILL.md. No exceptions.

Context window is memory. Manage it.

Section titled “Context window is memory. Manage it.”

The guide calls it “Just-in-Time Loading.” Don’t pull references into context until the agent needs them. Keep SKILL.md lean: procedures and navigation only. Move schemas, API docs, and cheatsheets to references/. Move templates to assets/. Tell the agent explicitly when to read each file: “See references/auth-flow.md for specific error codes.”

Flat subdirectories only. One level deep. references/schema.md works. references/db/v1/schema.md doesn’t. This keeps the mental model simple for both you and the agent.

This is memory management for a runtime that charges per token.

Write for machines, not humans

Section titled “Write for machines, not humans”

Three rules that change how you author skill instructions:

Step-by-step numbering. Define workflows as strict chronological sequences. Map decision trees explicitly: “Step 2: If you need source maps run ng build --source-map. Otherwise, skip to Step 3.” No ambiguity. No room for creative interpretation.

Concrete templates over prose. Agents pattern-match well. A JSON template in assets/ beats paragraphs describing what the output should look like. Don’t describe — show.

Third-person imperative. “Extract the text…” not “You should extract…” or “I will extract…” This framing produces more consistent agent behavior.

Pick one term per concept and stick with it. Use domain-native vocabulary. In Angular, say “template” — not “html”, “markup”, or “view.” Consistency reduces the chance of the agent conflating similar concepts.

Offload fragile work to scripts

Section titled “Offload fragile work to scripts”

Don’t ask an LLM to write complex parsing logic from scratch every time a skill runs. Give it a tested Python or Bash script in the scripts/ directory. Design scripts as tiny CLIs.

The critical detail: make scripts return descriptive, human-readable error messages on stdout/stderr. When a script fails with “Error: Unable to resolve CommonJS dependency ‘lodash’ — try adding it to the Vite optimizeDeps.include array,” the agent can self-correct. When it fails with exit code 1 and no message, the agent is stuck.

Don’t create files that waste tokens

Section titled “Don’t create files that waste tokens”

Skills are for agents, not humans. The guide is explicit about what NOT to create:

  • Documentation files: No README.md, CHANGELOG.md, or INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md
  • Redundant logic: If the agent already handles a task reliably, delete the instruction
  • Library code: Skills contain tiny, single-purpose scripts. Long-lived libraries belong elsewhere

Every file in a skill directory consumes context. Be ruthless about what earns its place.

Test skills with LLMs

Section titled “Test skills with LLMs”

This is where the guide separates itself from typical “best practices” lists.

Discovery validation. Paste your YAML frontmatter into a fresh LLM chat. Ask it to generate three prompts that should trigger the skill and three that shouldn’t. If the description can’t discriminate between them, rewrite it. Then go further — prompt agents with real assignments and inspect which skills they chose and why.

Logic validation. Feed the LLM your entire SKILL.md and directory tree. Have it simulate execution step-by-step against a concrete task. For each step, it writes out what it’s doing, which file it’s reading or running, and — critically — flags every point where your instructions force it to guess. These are “execution blockers”: ambiguities that will produce inconsistent results in production.

Adversarial testing. Switch roles. Make the LLM attack your skill as a QA tester. “What if the esbuild script fails on a CommonJS dependency? What if the user’s angular.json has custom Webpack builders that Vite doesn’t support? What assumptions am I making about the Node environment?” Don’t fix anything yet — just collect the questions.

Architecture refinement. After answering the adversarial questions, have the LLM restructure your skill. Push dense content out of SKILL.md into references/ and assets/. Add error handling sections. Enforce progressive disclosure so the context window stays lean.

The guide also points to SkillsBench — a benchmark for evaluating skills — as inspiration for building your own evals.

The endgame

Section titled “The endgame”

Gechev’s repo includes a meta-skill: a skill that creates other skills. That’s the direction this is heading. Agents writing instructions for agents, validated by agents.

We’re not there yet. But treating skills as first-class software artifacts — with architecture, testing, and deployment discipline — is the difference between an agent that occasionally helps and one that reliably ships.

Quick reference

Section titled “Quick reference”
PrincipleRule
StructureSKILL.md + scripts/ + references/ + assets/
SKILL.md sizeUnder 500 lines
SubdirectoriesFlat, one level deep
DiscoveryTrigger-optimized description with negative triggers
LoadingJust-in-time, not upfront
InstructionsThird-person imperative, step-by-step
TemplatesConcrete examples over prose descriptions
ScriptsTiny CLIs with descriptive error messages
ValidationLLM-driven: discovery, logic, adversarial, refinement
WasteNo README, no changelog, no library code

References

Section titled “References”
  • mgechev/skills-best-practices — The source repo
  • Claude Agent Skills Best Practices — Official documentation
  • SkillsBench — Benchmark for evaluating agent skills

Claude Code 2.1.41–2.1.63: Eight Releases, Fifteen Days, One Platform Shift

Mar 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.41–2.1.63: Eight Releases, Fifteen Days, One Platform Shift

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.41–2.1.63: Eight Releases, Fifteen Days, One Platform Shift”

Eight releases in fifteen days. If you blinked between February 13 and February 28, you missed Claude Code growing from a terminal coding assistant into something that looks a lot more like a multi-agent development platform — complete with team coordination, isolated workspaces, and the ability to watch your AI agents work from your phone.

Here’s what actually shipped, and why the pieces fit together in a way the individual changelog entries don’t reveal.

The Foundation: Auth and Sessions

Section titled “The Foundation: Auth and Sessions”

v2.1.41 (Feb 13)

claude auth login, claude auth status, claude auth logout. Basic CLI plumbing. /rename now auto-generates session names from conversation context. Fixed @-mentions with anchor fragments.

Small things. But they signal a tool that expects you to run multiple sessions and manage them properly.

New Brains: Sonnet 4.6

Section titled “New Brains: Sonnet 4.6”

v2.1.45 (Feb 17)

Sonnet 4.6 arrived. Opus 4.6 had been shipping since v2.1.32 (Feb 5) with 1M context and fast mode. With 2.1.45, the model lineup solidified:

ModelRolePricing (in/out per Mtok)
Opus 4.6Deep work, complex reasoning$5 / $25 (standard), $10 / $37.50 (1M context)
Sonnet 4.6Daily driving, balanced$3 / $15
Haiku 4.5Speed tasks, sub-agents$1 / $5

Also in this release: spinnerTipsOverride for custom spinner messages, and SDK rate limit types (SDKRateLimitInfo, SDKRateLimitEvent) for consumers to monitor utilization.

Agent Lifecycle Primitives

Section titled “Agent Lifecycle Primitives”

v2.1.47 (Feb 17)

This is where it gets interesting. Background agents got proper lifecycle management:

  • Ctrl+F to kill all background agents (replaced double-ESC, which now only cancels the main thread)
  • Shift+Down with wrapping for teammate navigation (simplified from Shift+Up/Down)
  • last_assistant_message field in Stop and SubagentStop hook inputs — hooks can access the final response without parsing transcripts
  • /rename updates the terminal tab title

These aren’t user-facing features. They’re operating system primitives for multi-agent coordination.

v2.1.49 (Feb 20)

The agent architecture expanded:

  • --worktree (-w) flag to start Claude in an isolated git worktree
  • Subagents support isolation: "worktree" for their own isolated workspaces
  • Ctrl+F keybinding to kill background agents (two-press confirmation)
  • Agent definitions support background: true to always run as background tasks
  • Plugins can ship settings.json for default configuration
  • CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE mode now includes the file edit tool
  • ConfigChange hook event for security auditing of settings changes
  • Sonnet 4.5 with 1M context removed from Max plan — Sonnet 4.6 takes over

Worktree Isolation for Agents

Section titled “Worktree Isolation for Agents”

v2.1.50 (Feb 21)

This solves the fundamental problem of parallel agents: if three agents are editing code simultaneously, they’ll create merge conflicts. Worktree isolation gives each agent its own branch and working directory.

  • isolation: worktree in agent definitions — declarative worktree isolation
  • WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove hook events for custom VCS setup/teardown
  • claude agents CLI command to list all configured agents
  • CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT env var
  • Opus 4.6 fast mode now includes full 1M context window
  • CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE mode disables MCP tools, attachments, hooks, and CLAUDE.md

Persistent Agent Memory

Section titled “Persistent Agent Memory”

v2.1.35 (Feb 6) → v2.1.50

The memory frontmatter field for agents. Three scopes: user, project, local. Your code reviewer can remember patterns it discovered last week. Your architect agent accumulates knowledge about your codebase across conversations. The agents aren’t stateless anymore.

Agent Teams — Research Preview

Section titled “Agent Teams — Research Preview”

v2.1.32 (Feb 5) → v2.1.50

Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 and you can spawn coordinated teams:

Three reviewers, each with a different lens — security, performance, test coverage — working in parallel and reporting findings. Token-intensive, but the coordination patterns are real.

Related primitives that landed:

  • TeammateIdle and TaskCompleted hook events (v2.1.35)
  • Restrict which subagents can be spawned via Task(agent_type) syntax (v2.1.35)
  • “Summarize from here” in the message selector (v2.1.32)
  • Skills from --add-dir directories auto-load (v2.1.32)
  • Skill character budget scales with context window — 2% of context (v2.1.32)

Remote Control

Section titled “Remote Control”

v2.1.51 (Feb 23)

Start a Claude Code session on your machine. Pick it up from your phone, tablet, or another browser.

Works with claude.ai/code and the Claude mobile app. The constraint of “sitting at the terminal” disappears.

Also in this release:

  • Plugin marketplace git timeout increased from 30s to 120s (configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_GIT_TIMEOUT_MS)
  • Custom npm registries and specific version pinning for plugin installation
  • BashTool skips login shell by default when shell snapshot is available (previously required CLAUDE_BASH_NO_LOGIN=true)
  • CLAUDE_CODE_ACCOUNT_UUID, CLAUDE_CODE_USER_EMAIL, CLAUDE_CODE_ORGANIZATION_UUID env vars for SDK account info

Platform Convergence

Section titled “Platform Convergence”

v2.1.63 (Feb 28)

The boundaries between claude.ai web and Claude Code CLI dissolve:

  • claude.ai MCP servers available in CLI — MCP connectors configured in your claude.ai account work automatically in Claude Code. Opt out with ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false.
  • HTTP hooks — POST JSON to a URL instead of running shell commands. Headers support env var expansion.
  • /simplify and /batch ship as bundled slash commands
  • Project configs and auto memory shared across git worktrees
  • “Always copy full response” option in /copy picker

The Architecture, Visible

Section titled “The Architecture, Visible”

Read together, in fifteen days Claude Code added:

LayerWhat shippedVersion
ModelOpus 4.6 + Sonnet 4.6 with 1M context, fast mode2.1.32–2.1.45
Isolation--worktree flag, agent isolation: worktree, WorktreeCreate/Remove hooks2.1.49–2.1.50
CoordinationAgent teams, TeammateIdle/TaskCompleted hooks, background agent lifecycle2.1.32–2.1.50
MemoryPersistent agent memory (user/project/local scope)2.1.35–2.1.50
ConnectivityRemote control, claude.ai MCP bridge, HTTP hooks2.1.51–2.1.63

That’s not a patch cycle. That’s a platform forming.

What to Try First

Section titled “What to Try First”
  1. Worktree isolation: claude -w my-feature — work in a clean branch without affecting main
  2. Agent teams: Enable CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, spawn three specialized reviewers on your next PR
  3. Remote control: claude remote-control — start a task, then pick it up from your phone
  4. Persistent memory: Add memory: project to your agent definitions and watch them learn your codebase
  5. HTTP hooks: Replace shell-based hooks with HTTP endpoints for better integration with your toolchain

myclaude: Stop Switching AI Tools — Let Claude Code Orchestrate Them All

Mar 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

myclaude: Stop Switching AI Tools — Let Claude Code Orchestrate Them All

Section titled “myclaude: Stop Switching AI Tools — Let Claude Code Orchestrate Them All”

You have Claude Code open in one terminal. Codex in another. Maybe Gemini CLI in a third. Each one handles something different. But every time you switch, you lose context, re-explain your intent, and break your flow.

What if Claude Code could just delegate? Send the coding task to Codex while it keeps planning the next step?

That’s myclaude. One orchestrator, multiple executors, zero context loss.

What myclaude Does

Section titled “What myclaude Does”

myclaude is an open-source framework (2.4k stars, 74 releases) that turns Claude Code into an orchestration layer. Instead of replacing your AI coding tools, it coordinates them.

The architecture splits AI coding into two roles:

RoleAgentResponsibility
OrchestratorClaude CodePlanning, context gathering, verification
Executorcodeagent-wrapperCode editing, test execution via any backend

The codeagent-wrapper is a unified execution layer. It routes tasks to whichever backend you’ve configured — Codex, Claude, Gemini, or OpenCode — and normalizes the output. Each backend has different protocols:

BackendProtocol
Codexcodex e, --json, -C, resume
Claude--output-format stream-json, -r
Gemini-o stream-json, -y, -r
OpenCodeopencode, stdin mode

The wrapper handles all of that, so Claude Code just sends tasks and gets structured results back.

Installation

Section titled “Installation”

One command:

The installer walks you through module selection. It detects already-installed modules and only updates what’s changed.

After installation, your ~/.claude/ directory looks like this:

Modules: Pick What You Need

Section titled “Modules: Pick What You Need”

myclaude doesn’t ship a monolithic platform. You choose from 8 modules:

ModuleCommandWhat It Does
do/do5-phase feature development with codeagent orchestration
omo/omoMulti-agent orchestration with intelligent routing
bmad/bmad-pilotBMAD agile workflow with 6 specialized agents
requirements/requirements-pilotLightweight requirements-to-code pipeline
essentials/code, /debug, etc.11 core dev commands
sparv/sparvSpecify→Plan→Act→Review→Vault workflow
coursecompositeCombines dev + product-requirements + test-cases
claudekitcompositedo skill + global hooks

Enable or disable modules in config.json:

Which Module to Start With

Section titled “Which Module to Start With”
ScenarioRecommended
Feature development/do
Bug investigation + fix/omo
Large enterprise project/bmad-pilot
Quick prototype/requirements-pilot
Simple, focused task/code, /debug

Daily Workflow Examples

Section titled “Daily Workflow Examples”

Feature Development with /do

Section titled “Feature Development with /do”

The /do module implements a 5-phase workflow:

  1. Specify — Define what you want to build
  2. Plan — Break it down into steps
  3. Act — Execute with codeagent orchestration (Claude Code plans, Codex/Gemini executes)
  4. Review — Verify the results
  5. Vault — Save knowledge for future reference

Each phase uses the orchestrator-executor split. Claude Code handles the thinking; the codeagent-wrapper handles the doing.

Bug Investigation with /omo

Section titled “Bug Investigation with /omo”

When you’re not sure which tool is best for the job, /omo decides for you. It analyzes the task, picks the right backend, and routes execution automatically. Good for debugging where you need different tools at different stages — Claude Code for analysis, Codex for quick fixes, Gemini for large-context searches.

Everyday Commands (Essentials)

Section titled “Everyday Commands (Essentials)”

The essentials module gives you 11 standalone commands:

  • /code — Generate code from a description
  • /debug — Investigate and fix issues
  • /test — Write and run tests
  • /review — Code review with feedback
  • /refactor — Restructure existing code
  • /docs — Generate documentation
  • /optimize — Performance improvements
  • /bugfix — Targeted bug fixes
  • /ask — Ask questions about the codebase
  • /think — Deep reasoning on a problem
  • /enhance-prompt — Improve your prompts

Each command is a workflow, not just a prompt template. It includes context gathering, execution, and verification steps.

Hook System

Section titled “Hook System”

myclaude includes a hook system that runs shell commands in response to events:

  • pre-bash — Inject context before bash execution
  • inject-spec — Auto-detect and inject task-specific specs
  • log-prompt — Log prompts for debugging and optimization

Hooks are configured in settings.json and run automatically during workflows.

Individual Skills

Section titled “Individual Skills”

Beyond modules, myclaude offers 9 individual skills that can be installed separately:

SkillDescription
browserBrowser automation for web testing
codeagentcodeagent-wrapper invocation for multi-backend tasks
codexDirect Codex backend execution
devLightweight end-to-end development workflow
geminiDirect Gemini backend execution
product-requirementsInteractive PRD generation with quality scoring
prototype-prompt-generatorStructured UI/UX prototype prompt generation
skill-installInstall skills from GitHub with security scanning
test-casesComprehensive test case generation

FAQ & Troubleshooting

Section titled “FAQ & Troubleshooting”

Q: Do I need all backends installed? No. You only need the backends you want to use. If you only have Claude Code and Codex, configure those two and leave the rest.

Q: What happens if a backend CLI isn’t found? The codeagent-wrapper will report an error for that specific backend. Other backends continue to work. Check with:

Q: “Unknown event format” warning? A logging display issue. Can be safely ignored.

Q: Gemini can’t read .gitignore files? Known limitation. Remove from .gitignore or use a different backend for that task.

Q: Codex permission denied? Set approval_policy = "never" in ~/.codex/config.yaml.

Q: How do I update?

This detects already-installed modules and updates only changed files.

How It Compares

Section titled “How It Compares”
FeaturemyclaudeaiderContinue.devCursor
Multi-backend orchestrationYes (4 backends)No (single LLM)NoNo
Modular modules8 modulesMonolithicExtension-basedMonolithic
CLI-nativeYesYesIDE extensionIDE
Structured workflowsYes (/do, /sparv)NoNoNo
Open sourceAGPL-3.0Apache-2.0Apache-2.0Proprietary
GitHub stars2.4k30k+20k+N/A

myclaude fills a different niche. It’s not competing with IDE-integrated tools like Cursor or Continue. It’s designed for developers who live in the terminal, use Claude Code as their primary tool, and want to leverage other AI backends without switching context.

The Numbers

  • 2.4k GitHub stars, 275 forks
  • 325 commits across the codebase
  • 74 releases (latest: v6.8.2, March 3, 2026)

Select your modules. Configure your backends. Start with /do for feature development or /code for quick tasks.

The Coding Agent Harness: Why Context Engineering Beats Model Shopping

Mar 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Coding Agent Harness: Why Context Engineering Beats Model Shopping

Section titled “The Coding Agent Harness: Why Context Engineering Beats Model Shopping”

Your team adopted an AI coding agent last month. The first week felt electric. By week three, the pattern became clear: sometimes the agent nails it, sometimes it produces code that looks plausible but crumbles under review. Duplicate logic in three places. A helper function recreated from scratch when one already exists in utils. An N+1 query hiding inside a loop.

You start wondering if you picked the wrong model.

You didn’t. The model was never the problem.

The Insight Most Teams Miss

Section titled “The Insight Most Teams Miss”

Julian de Angelis at MercadoLibre has been deploying AI coding agents across nearly 20,000 developers and thousands of repositories. His conclusion after operating at that scale:

Your AI coding agent is a brilliant new hire on day one. Fast, eager, and with zero context about your codebase, your conventions, or your architecture.

You wouldn’t hand a new engineer a Jira ticket that says “fix this bug” and walk away. You’d onboard them: docs, tech stack overview, style guides, release workflows, access to internal tools, a mentor to review their work.

That onboarding system is what de Angelis calls the agent harness - the structured set of controls that shape what the agent knows, what it can do, and how its work gets validated. The underlying discipline is context engineering: designing and controlling everything an LLM sees before it generates a single token.

The Constraint Nobody Talks About

Section titled “The Constraint Nobody Talks About”

Every popular AI coding agent - Claude Code, Cursor, Codex - runs the same fundamental loop:

Read -> Plan -> Code -> Validate -> Iterate

The agent reads your files, plans an approach, writes code, runs tests, and loops back if something fails. At every iteration, the context window grows. System prompts, tool definitions, conversation history, file contents, terminal output, the agent’s own generated code - all of it accumulates in a finite workspace.

Here’s the part that surprises people: past roughly 60% utilization of the context window, more context makes the agent actively worse. This phenomenon is called context rot. Even with windows reaching 1M tokens, the fundamental challenge remains. Every token spent on a verbose tool result or an overly long rules file is a token not available for the actual task.

The best agent harnesses are designed with this reality at the center: inject the right context at the right moment, and avoid polluting the window with anything else.

Four Levers That Actually Matter

Section titled “Four Levers That Actually Matter”

1. Custom Rules

Section titled “1. Custom Rules”

Files like CLAUDE.md, cursor/rules, or AGENTS.md get injected into the agent’s context at the start of every interaction. This is the most accessible lever.

What goes in:

  • Tech stack and architecture patterns
  • Naming conventions and code style
  • Testing philosophy (“always write unit tests with table-driven inputs”)
  • Common pitfalls specific to your codebase
  • Anti-patterns you’ve seen the agent produce repeatedly

What doesn’t belong:

  • Entire API documentation (too long, wastes context)
  • Obvious instructions (“write clean code”)
  • Contradictory rules

Practical tips:

  • Keep them under 500 lines. Precision matters.
  • Split rules into focused files by concern: architecture, testing, code style, security. The agent loads only what’s relevant.
  • Include few-shot examples. Models learn from examples better than abstract instructions.
  • Make them living documents. Every time the agent makes a mistake, update the rules. Over weeks, this file becomes remarkably effective.

2. MCP Servers

Section titled “2. MCP Servers”

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers are plugins that give the agent tools beyond reading and writing files. Without them, the agent is limited to what’s in the repo. With them, it can:

  • Query your database to understand schema and data
  • Search internal documentation or wikis
  • Look up API contracts
  • Interact with CI/CD pipelines
  • Access design specs from Figma
  • Validate its own output against real systems

MCP servers bridge the gap between the agent and your organization’s knowledge. They give the agent access to the same resources a human developer would use.

3. Skills

Section titled “3. Skills”

Skills give the agent new capabilities and domain expertise. A skill is a directory with an entrypoint file that can bundle templates, example outputs, reference docs, and executable scripts.

The design is clever: only a short description stays in context permanently, so the agent knows what’s available. The full content loads only when the skill is invoked - by the user or automatically when the agent detects relevance. This on-demand loading means skills can be as detailed as needed without permanently consuming context budget.

They come in two flavors:

  • Reference skills inject knowledge: conventions, patterns, domain context
  • Task skills provide step-by-step instructions for specific actions

The real power is that skills can bundle and execute scripts, run in isolated subagents with their own clean context window, and compose together. Programmable, context-aware, composable units of agent behavior.

4. Spec-Driven Development

Section titled “4. Spec-Driven Development”

This one reframes how you interact with agents entirely.

Consider this prompt: “Make a new feature to add new items from the backoffice.”

Seems simple. But it says nothing about: which tech stack, where the backoffice is, API contracts, storage layer, idempotency handling, authorization rules.

The agent will read the codebase, plan something reasonable, and produce a working MVP. You add an item and it works. You click “add” again and it inserts the item twice. It was “obvious” the agent should have managed idempotency by ID. In your business, it’s “obvious” that only one role can insert items.

The problem isn’t the agent. It’s the bare initial input. The bottleneck sits between the chair and the screen.

Spec-Driven Development (SDD) solves this by writing detailed specifications before the agent writes code. What the feature does, how it integrates, edge cases, acceptance criteria, test plans. The spec becomes the harness - it consolidates architecture decisions, guidance, and review criteria into a single artifact that engineers the agent’s entire context window in one shot.

And you can use the agent to write the specs too.

The Feedback Loop

Section titled “The Feedback Loop”

The four levers define what the agent knows and can do. The piece that makes the whole system converge is the feedback loop: tests, linters, type checkers, build scripts. Every tool that produces a pass/fail signal becomes a self-correction mechanism.

Agent hooks make this enforceable. They are user-defined commands that execute automatically at specific points in the agent’s lifecycle. Wire your validation into a Stop hook, and the agent literally cannot finish until the checks pass. Not a suggestion it might ignore. An enforced gate.

The more structured feedback available, the less human intervention is needed.

MercadoLibre’s Playbook at 20,000 Developers

Section titled “MercadoLibre’s Playbook at 20,000 Developers”

Theory is fine. Here’s what works at scale with 9+ technology stacks, thousands of legacy repositories, and multiple knowledge domains:

Standardized rules per technology. A curated set of custom rules at the org level, tuned to each tech stack, internal libraries, and code review standards. Teams inherit the base and layer on repo-specific rules. Getting the specificity right is critical - too specific breaks legacy projects, too loose lets unapproved libraries through (security risk).

Internal MCP servers. Built-in access to internal cloud platform capabilities, internal SDKs, business context via RAG, and updated application documentation.

Custom code review agents. Standalone review agents running in CI that analyze every PR - human-written or AI-generated - before a human reviewer sees it. They return prioritized findings so engineers see critical issues first. Human reviewers focus on design decisions instead of catching style violations. Faster review cycles, more consistent quality, and a safety net that scales with PR volume, not reviewer headcount.

Start Here

Section titled “Start Here”

If you haven’t built an agent harness yet, start with the simplest lever: custom rules. Create a CLAUDE.md or equivalent file with your coding conventions, common pitfalls, and a couple of concrete examples of good and bad patterns in your codebase.

Run it for a week. Every time the agent produces something wrong, add a rule. By the end of the month, that file will have quietly transformed your results more than any model upgrade could.

The teams that win with AI coding agents won’t be the ones using the fanciest model. They’ll be the ones with the best-engineered harness.

Based on Julian de Angelis’s analysis of AI coding agent deployment at MercadoLibre. Original thread.

  • Spec Driven Development
